kamelets.name: avro-deserialize-action
kamelets.title: Avro Deserialize Action
kamelets.summary: Turns each message of Avro binary data back into a JSON object, using the Avro schema the data was written with.
kamelets.description:
Turns each message of Avro binary data back into a JSON object, using the Avro schema the data was written with.

Use it to read records that arrive in Avro, a compact binary format described by a schema, for example from a Kafka topic, and work on them as JSON. To turn JSON into Avro, use `avro-serialize-action`; for Protobuf, use `protobuf-deserialize-action`.

Input: Avro binary data, as bytes, without the schema in it, such as `avro-serialize-action` writes.

Output: the body is parsed JSON (a Jackson `JsonNode`) with one field for each field of the schema. The `Content-Type` header is removed. Put `json-serialize-action` after this action to get JSON text.

Good to know: Avro data does not say which schema it was written with, so the schema must be the one the writer used. When `schema` is not set, the schema found by an earlier `resolve-pojo-schema-action` is used.

kamelets.name: avro-serialize-action
kamelets.title: Avro Serialize Action
kamelets.summary: Turns each message, a JSON object, into Avro binary data that follows the Avro schema you give.
kamelets.description:
Turns each message, a JSON object, into Avro binary data that follows the Avro schema you give.

Use it to send records in Avro, a compact binary format described by a schema, to a system that expects it, such as a Kafka topic whose readers decode Avro. To turn Avro back into JSON, use `avro-deserialize-action`; for Protobuf, use `protobuf-serialize-action`.

Input: parsed JSON (a Map or a Jackson `JsonNode`) whose fields match the schema. JSON text fails: put `json-deserialize-action` before this action to parse it.

Output: the body is the Avro binary data, as bytes, and the `Content-Type` header is set to `application/avro`.

Good to know: the schema is not written into the data, so whoever reads it needs the same schema. A message fails when it lacks a field of the schema, has a field the schema does not know, or has a value of the wrong type. When `schema` is not set, the schema found by an earlier `resolve-pojo-schema-action` is used.

kamelets.summary: Reads the events that AWS CloudTrail records in an AWS account, such as API calls and console sign-ins, one message per event.
kamelets.description:
Reads the events that AWS CloudTrail records in an AWS account, such as API calls and console sign-ins, one message per event.

Use it to react to activity in an AWS account, for example to raise an alert when a secret is read, a security group is changed or someone signs in to the console. Set `eventSource` to read the events of one AWS service only.

Output: the body is the CloudTrail record of the event, as JSON text. The headers give the ID, the name (such as `GetSecretValue`), the source (such as `secretsmanager.amazonaws.com`) and the user name of the event.

Good to know: it looks up the management events that CloudTrail keeps for the region, which go back 90 days, so when it starts it also reads events from before. It remembers which events it read only while it runs: after a restart it reads them again. Nothing is removed from CloudTrail. An event can be looked up only some minutes after it happened.

kamelets.name: aws-cloudwatch-sink
kamelets.title: AWS CloudWatch Metrics Sink
kamelets.summary: Sends one data point of a custom metric to Amazon CloudWatch for each message, with the name, the value and the unit of the metric taken from headers.
kamelets.description:
Sends one data point of a custom metric to Amazon CloudWatch for each message, with the name, the value and the unit of the metric taken from headers.

Use it to record business or technical numbers from an integration, such as orders processed, items in stock or processing time, and to graph them or set alarms on them in CloudWatch.

Input: the body is not used. The `metric-name` header (or `ce-metricname`) is the name of the metric, and is required. The optional `metric-value` header (or `ce-metricvalue`) is the value, a number, 1 when it is not set. The optional `metric-unit` header (or `ce-metricunit`) is the unit, such as `Count`, `Seconds`, `Bytes` or `Percent`, `Count` when it is not set. The optional `metric-dimension-name` and `metric-dimension-value` headers (or `ce-metricdimensionname` and `ce-metricdimensionvalue`) add one dimension, such as `Region` and `eu`. The optional `metric-timestamp` header (or `ce-metrictimestamp`) is the time of the data point.

Output: the message is unchanged.

Good to know: a message without a metric name, or with a value that is not a number, fails. The time in `metric-timestamp` must be a Java `Instant` or `Date`: text is ignored, and then the data point gets the time it is sent.

kamelets.name: aws-eventbridge-sink
kamelets.title: AWS Eventbridge Sink
kamelets.summary: Sends each message as an event to an Amazon EventBridge event bus, where rules route it to targets such as Lambda functions, SQS queues or Step Functions.
kamelets.description:
Sends each message as an event to an Amazon EventBridge event bus, where rules route it to targets such as Lambda functions, SQS queues or Step Functions.

Use it to publish business events, such as `Order Shipped`, for other applications and AWS services to react to through EventBridge rules.

Input: the body is the detail of the event, as JSON text that holds a JSON object, such as `{"orderId": "A-1"}`. The `detail-type` header (or `ce-detail-type`) is the detail type, such as `Order Shipped`; the `event-source` header (or `ce-event-source`, or `ce-source`) is the source, such as `com.example.shop`; and the `resources-arn` header (or `ce-resources-arn`) is the ARN (Amazon Resource Name) of the resource the event is about, or several separated by commas. Each header falls back on its option: `detailType`, `eventSource` and `resourcesArn`.

Output: when it is used inside a route, the body afterwards is the response of EventBridge, and the `CamelAwsEventbridgeFailedEntryCount` header is 1 when EventBridge rejected the event, 0 otherwise.

Good to know: a message fails when it has no detail type, no source or no resource ARN, from a header or an option. `eventSourcePrefix` is put before every source. An event that EventBridge rejects, such as one whose body is not a JSON object, is not delivered; depending on the Camel version the message then fails, or it only sets `CamelAwsEventbridgeFailedEntryCount` to 1.

kamelets.name: aws-kinesis-firehose-sink
kamelets.title: AWS Kinesis Firehose Sink
kamelets.summary: Sends each message as a record to an Amazon Data Firehose (Kinesis Data Firehose) delivery stream, which delivers the records in batches to S3, Redshift, OpenSearch or another service.
kamelets.description:
Sends each message as a record to an Amazon Data Firehose (Kinesis Data Firehose) delivery stream, which delivers the records in batches to S3, Redshift, OpenSearch or another service.

Use it to load events or logs into S3 or a data warehouse without writing code that reads them, with Firehose doing the batching. To feed a Kinesis data stream that your own applications read, use `aws-kinesis-sink`.

Input: the body becomes the data of the record, as text, bytes or a stream. Turn structured data such as a Map into JSON text first, for example with `json-serialize-action`. Firehose writes the records one after the other, without anything between them: end each record with a line break if the files must have one record per line. Headers are not used.

Output: the message is unchanged. The `CamelAwsKinesisFirehoseRecordId` header gives the ID of the record.

Good to know: the delivery stream must exist and take Direct PUT as its source; a message for a delivery stream that does not exist fails.

kamelets.name: aws-kinesis-sink
kamelets.title: AWS Kinesis Sink
kamelets.summary: Writes each message as a record to an Amazon Kinesis data stream.
kamelets.description:
Writes each message as a record to an Amazon Kinesis data stream.

Use it to feed a stream of events, such as clicks, logs or sensor readings, to the applications that read the stream, for example with `aws-kinesis-source`. To deliver data to S3 or a data warehouse without writing a reader, use `aws-kinesis-firehose-sink`.

Input: the body becomes the data of the record, as text, bytes or a stream. The optional `partition` header (or `ce-partition`) is the partition key: the records with the same key go to the same shard, in order. Without it, the key is a unique ID, so the records spread over the shards. The optional `sequence-number` header (or `ce-sequencenumber`) is the sequence number of the record that must come before this one, for a strict order within a partition key.

Output: the message is unchanged. The `CamelAwsKinesisSequenceNumber` and `CamelAwsKinesisShardId` headers give the sequence number and the shard of the record.

Good to know: the stream must exist. The other headers are not sent: a Kinesis record has only data and a partition key.

kamelets.name: aws-kinesis-source
kamelets.title: AWS Kinesis Source
kamelets.summary: Reads the records of an Amazon Kinesis data stream, one message per record.
kamelets.description:
Reads the records of an Amazon Kinesis data stream, one message per record.

Use it to process a stream of events that other applications write to Kinesis, such as clicks, logs or readings from devices, for example with `aws-kinesis-sink`.

Output: the body is the data of the record, as bytes. The headers give the partition key, the sequence number, the shard ID and the arrival time of the record.

Good to know: it reads the stream from its oldest record, and again from the oldest record each time the integration starts: it does not remember where it stopped, so records are read again after a restart. Records are not removed: Kinesis keeps them for the retention period of the stream. With `useKclConsumers` it reads through the Kinesis Client Library instead, and the body is a `ByteBuffer` rather than bytes.

kamelets.name: aws-s3-event-based-source
kamelets.title: AWS S3 Event Based Source
kamelets.summary: Receives the events of an Amazon S3 bucket, such as a new or a deleted file, from the Amazon SQS queue that Amazon EventBridge sends them to, one message per event.
kamelets.description:
Receives the events of an Amazon S3 bucket, such as a new or a deleted file, from the Amazon SQS queue that Amazon EventBridge sends them to, one message per event.

Use it to react to new files in a bucket as soon as they arrive, without listing the bucket again and again, for example to process uploaded documents or imported data files. To read the files of a bucket by polling it, use `aws-s3-source`.

Output: the body is the EventBridge event, as JSON text: `detail-type` says what happened (such as `Object Created` or `Object Deleted`), `detail.bucket.name` is the bucket and `detail.object.key` the key of the file. With `getObject` set to true, the event of a file uploaded with a simple upload (PutObject) carries the content of the file instead, as a stream, with the `CamelAwsS3ProducedBucketName` and `CamelAwsS3ProducedKey` headers; the other events then come as parsed JSON (a Jackson `JsonNode`).

Good to know: it needs a setup in AWS. In the properties of the bucket, turn on sending events to Amazon EventBridge; then create an EventBridge rule for the events of source `aws.s3` and that bucket, with the queue as its target. Each event is deleted from the queue once it has been processed, unless `deleteAfterRead` is false. The files stay in the bucket. `getObject` skips files created by a multipart upload or a copy, and never connects through `uriEndpointOverride`.

kamelets.name: aws-s3-sink
kamelets.title: AWS S3 Sink
kamelets.summary: Uploads each message as a file (object) to an Amazon S3 bucket, under a key (file name) taken from a header, the `keyName` option, or a generated ID.
kamelets.description:
Uploads each message as a file (object) to an Amazon S3 bucket, under a key (file name) taken from a header, the `keyName` option, or a generated ID.

Use it to store data in S3 for other systems or for archiving, such as exported records, received documents or events. To collect many small messages into a few large files, use `aws-s3-streaming-upload-sink`.

Input: the body is the content of the file, as text, bytes, a stream or a file. Turn structured data such as a Map into JSON text first, for example with `json-serialize-action`. The optional `file` header (or `ce-file`) is the key, the path of the file in the bucket, such as `orders/order-1.json`. Without it, and without `keyName`, the key is a generated unique ID. The optional `CamelAwsS3ContentType` header sets the content type of the file; the `Content-Type` header is not used, and without it the file is stored as `application/octet-stream`.

Output: the message is unchanged. The `CamelAwsS3Key` and `CamelAwsS3ETag` headers give the key and the ETag of the uploaded file.

Good to know: a file with the same key is replaced without warning. When `keyName` is set, the `file` header is ignored and every message replaces the same file. To copy files from `aws-s3-source` under their own names, set the `file` header from its `CamelAwsS3Key` header first. It also works with S3-compatible storage, such as MinIO, through `overrideEndpoint`, `uriEndpointOverride` and `forcePathStyle`.

kamelets.name: aws-s3-source
kamelets.title: AWS S3 Source
kamelets.summary: Reads the files (objects) in an Amazon S3 bucket, one message per file, and by default deletes each file once it has been read.
kamelets.description:
Reads the files (objects) in an Amazon S3 bucket, one message per file, and by default deletes each file once it has been read.

Use it to process files that another system drops into a bucket, such as uploaded documents, exported reports or log files. To react to new files through S3 event notifications instead of reading the bucket over and over, use `aws-s3-event-based-source`.

Output: the body is the content of the file, as bytes. The headers give the bucket name, the key (the path of the file in the bucket), the content type and the ETag of the file.

Good to know: files are deleted from the bucket after they are read, unless `deleteAfterRead` is set to false; then the same files are read again on every poll. `moveAfterRead` moves them to another bucket instead. It also works with S3-compatible storage, such as MinIO, through `overrideEndpoint` and `uriEndpointOverride`.

kamelets.name: aws-s3-streaming-upload-sink
kamelets.title: AWS S3 Streaming upload Sink
kamelets.summary: Writes many messages into a few large files in an Amazon S3 bucket, adding each message to the current file and starting a new file after a number of messages or bytes.
kamelets.description:
Writes many messages into a few large files in an Amazon S3 bucket, adding each message to the current file and starting a new file after a number of messages or bytes.

Use it to store a stream of small records, such as log lines, events or sensor readings, as a few large files instead of one file per message. To upload one file per message, use `aws-s3-sink`.

Input: the body is added to the end of the current file as it is, as text, bytes or a stream. Nothing is put between two messages: end each message with a line break if the file must have one record per line. Headers are not used: the names of the files come from `keyName`.

Output: the message is unchanged. The message that completes a file gets the `CamelAwsS3ETag` header of that file.

Good to know: a file is uploaded when it has `batchMessageNumber` messages or `batchSize` bytes, or when `streamingUploadTimeout` has passed; until then it is not in the bucket. With the default `namingStrategy` of `progressive`, the first file is named `keyName`, such as `logs/app.log`, and the next ones `logs/app-1.log`, `logs/app-2.log` and so on. With `restartingPolicy` set to `override`, a new run starts again from `keyName` and replaces the files of the earlier run.

kamelets.description: Create a secret in AWS Secrets Manager.

kamelets.name: aws-ses-sink
kamelets.title: AWS SES Sink
kamelets.summary: Sends each message as a plain-text email through Amazon SES (Simple Email Service), to the addresses in the `to` header.
kamelets.description:
Sends each message as a plain-text email through Amazon SES (Simple Email Service), to the addresses in the `to` header.

Use it to send notifications, alerts or confirmations by email from an integration, such as an order confirmation or an alert when a job fails.

Input: the body is the text of the email, as plain text. The `to` header (or `ce-to`) is required: one or more recipient addresses, separated by commas. The optional `subject` header (or `ce-subject`) is the subject; without it, the subject is a generated ID. The optional `reply-to-addresses` header (or `ce-reply-to-addresses`) is a comma-separated list of addresses that replies go to.

Output: the message is unchanged. The `CamelAwsSesMessageId` header gives the ID that SES gave the email.

Good to know: a message without a `to` header fails. The `from` address must be verified in SES, and while the SES account is in the sandbox, the recipients must be verified too.

kamelets.name: aws-sns-fifo-sink
kamelets.title: AWS SNS FIFO Sink
kamelets.summary: Publishes each message to an Amazon SNS FIFO topic, which delivers the messages of a group in order, and without duplicates, to the SQS FIFO queues subscribed to it.
kamelets.description:
Publishes each message to an Amazon SNS FIFO topic, which delivers the messages of a group in order, and without duplicates, to the SQS FIFO queues subscribed to it.

Use it to fan out ordered updates, such as the changes of one order or one account, to several FIFO queues at once. For a standard topic use `aws-sns-sink`.

Input: the body becomes the text of the notification, as text. The optional `group` header (or `ce-group`) is the message group ID, such as a customer ID: the messages of one group are delivered in order. Without it, each message is a group of its own. The optional `subject` header (or `ce-subject`) is the subject. The other headers of the message, except the Camel ones, are sent as SNS message attributes.

Output: the message is unchanged. The `CamelAwsSnsMessageId` header gives the ID of the published message.

Good to know: the name of the topic ends in `.fifo`. With `contentBasedDeduplication` false, the default, each message gets a unique deduplication ID, so SNS drops only a message sent twice by a retry; set it to true to drop messages with the same body, which the topic must allow.

kamelets.name: aws-sns-sink
kamelets.title: AWS SNS Sink
kamelets.summary: Publishes each message to an Amazon SNS topic, which delivers it to every subscriber of the topic, such as SQS queues, Lambda functions, HTTP addresses, email addresses or phone numbers.
kamelets.description:
Publishes each message to an Amazon SNS topic, which delivers it to every subscriber of the topic, such as SQS queues, Lambda functions, HTTP addresses, email addresses or phone numbers.

Use it to fan out an event to many receivers at once, or to send notifications such as alerts by email or SMS through a topic. For a FIFO topic use `aws-sns-fifo-sink`; to send to a single queue use `aws-sqs-sink`.

Input: the body becomes the text of the notification, as text. Turn structured data such as a Map into JSON text first, for example with `json-serialize-action`. The optional `subject` header (or `ce-subject`) is the subject, which email subscribers see as the subject line. The other headers of the message, except the Camel ones, are sent as SNS message attributes.

Output: the message is unchanged. The `CamelAwsSnsMessageId` header gives the ID of the published message.

kamelets.name: aws-sqs-batch-sink
kamelets.title: AWS SQS Batch Sink
kamelets.summary: Splits the text of each message at a separator and sends the parts as separate SQS messages to an Amazon SQS queue, in one batch call.
kamelets.description:
Splits the text of each message at a separator and sends the parts as separate SQS messages to an Amazon SQS queue, in one batch call.

Use it to send many small items that arrive together, such as a comma-separated list of IDs, as one SQS message each, with fewer calls to AWS. To send each message as one SQS message, use `aws-sqs-sink`.

Input: the body is text that `batchSeparator` splits, such as `one,two,three` with a separator of `,`; each part becomes the body of one SQS message.

Output: when it is used inside a route, the body afterwards is the response of SQS, and the `CamelAwsSqsSuccessfulMessageCount` and `CamelAwsSqsFailedMessageCount` headers say how many parts were sent and how many failed.

Good to know: the queue is looked up by listing the queues, which needs the `sqs:ListQueues` permission besides `sqs:SendMessage`.

kamelets.name: aws-sqs-fifo-sink
kamelets.title: AWS SQS FIFO Sink
kamelets.summary: Sends each message to an Amazon SQS FIFO queue, which delivers the messages of a group in the order they were sent and drops duplicates.
kamelets.description:
Sends each message to an Amazon SQS FIFO queue, which delivers the messages of a group in the order they were sent and drops duplicates.

Use it to queue messages whose order matters, such as the updates of one order or one account, which must be processed in the order they happened. For a standard queue use `aws-sqs-sink`.

Input: the body becomes the body of the SQS message, as text. The optional `group` header (or `ce-group`) is the message group ID, such as a customer ID: the messages of one group are delivered in order. Without it, each message is a group of its own, so there is no order between messages.

Output: the message is unchanged. The `CamelAwsSqsMessageId` header gives the ID of the SQS message.

Good to know: the name of the queue ends in `.fifo`. With `contentBasedDeduplication` false, the default, each message gets a unique deduplication ID, so SQS drops only a message sent twice by a retry; set it to true to drop messages with the same body, which the queue must allow. The queue is looked up by listing the queues, which needs the `sqs:ListQueues` permission.

kamelets.name: aws-sqs-sink
kamelets.title: AWS SQS Sink
kamelets.summary: Sends each message as an SQS message to an Amazon SQS (Simple Queue Service) queue.
kamelets.description:
Sends each message as an SQS message to an Amazon SQS (Simple Queue Service) queue.

Use it to hand work to other systems that read the queue, such as orders to process or jobs to run, and to buffer it when they are slow or down. For a FIFO queue use `aws-sqs-fifo-sink`, to send many parts in one call use `aws-sqs-batch-sink`, and to notify many receivers at once use `aws-sns-sink`.

Input: the body becomes the body of the SQS message, as text; bytes and streams are read as text. Turn structured data such as a Map into JSON text first, for example with `json-serialize-action`. The other headers of the message, except the Camel ones, are sent as SQS message attributes.

Output: the message is unchanged. The `CamelAwsSqsMessageId` header gives the ID of the SQS message.

Good to know: the queue is looked up by listing the queues, which needs the `sqs:ListQueues` permission besides `sqs:SendMessage`. To reach a local stand-in of AWS, use `overrideEndpoint` and `uriEndpointOverride`.

kamelets.name: aws-sqs-source
kamelets.title: AWS SQS Source
kamelets.summary: Receives the messages of an Amazon SQS queue, one message each, and by default deletes each message from the queue once it has been processed.
kamelets.description:
Receives the messages of an Amazon SQS queue, one message each, and by default deletes each message from the queue once it has been processed.

Use it to process work that other systems put in a queue, such as orders, jobs or notifications, or the events that SNS, S3 or EventBridge send to a queue. For the events of an S3 bucket, `aws-s3-event-based-source` can also fetch the files.

Output: the body is the body of the SQS message, as text. The headers give the message ID (`CamelAwsSqsMessageId`), the receipt handle and the MD5 checksum of the body. The message attributes of the SQS message are not read.

Good to know: a message is deleted only after it has been processed without error; a message that fails stays in the queue and is received again when its visibility timeout ends. With `deleteAfterRead` set to false, the messages stay in the queue and are received again and again. Without `queueURL`, the queue is looked up by listing the queues, which needs the `sqs:ListQueues` permission.

kamelets.name: azure-cosmosdb-sink
kamelets.title: Azure CosmosDB Sink
kamelets.summary: Creates an item (a JSON document) in a container of Azure Cosmos DB for each message, from the JSON object in the body.
kamelets.description:
Creates an item (a JSON document) in a container of Azure Cosmos DB for each message, from the JSON object in the body.

Use it to store orders, events or profiles as JSON documents in Cosmos DB. To receive the changes made to a container, use `azure-cosmosdb-source`.

Input: the body is one item as JSON text: a JSON object with an `id` field, such as `{"id": "1001", "region": "EU"}`. A Map fails: turn it into JSON text first, for example with `json-serialize-action`. The partition key value of the item comes from the `itemPartitionKey` option or, when the option is not set, from the `itemPartitionKey` header (or `ce-itemPartitionKey`) of each message.

Output: the body afterwards is the item as it was created, as a Map, with the fields that Cosmos DB adds.

Good to know: a message without a partition key value fails, and so does an item whose `id` already exists in the same partition: the sink creates items and never replaces them.

kamelets.name: azure-cosmosdb-source
kamelets.title: Azure CosmosDB Source
kamelets.summary: Receives the items created or changed in a container of Azure Cosmos DB, through its change feed, as a JSON array per batch.
kamelets.description:
Receives the items created or changed in a container of Azure Cosmos DB, through its change feed, as a JSON array per batch.

Use it to react to new or updated documents, for example to copy them to a search index, a cache or Kafka. To create items, use `azure-cosmosdb-sink`.

Output: the body is a JSON array of the items of one batch, as bytes, each item with the fields that Cosmos DB adds, such as `_etag`.

Good to know: it reads only the changes made after it first starts, and it does not see deleted items. It keeps its position in a lease container, `camel-lease` in the database `databaseName` unless set otherwise, which must exist unless `createLeaseContainerIfNotExists` is true.

kamelets.name: azure-eventhubs-sink
kamelets.title: Azure Eventhubs Sink
kamelets.summary: Sends each message as an event to an event hub in Azure Event Hubs, the Azure service for event streams.
kamelets.description:
Sends each message as an event to an event hub in Azure Event Hubs, the Azure service for event streams.

Use it to publish events, such as clicks, sensor readings or changes, for stream processing or for other applications to read. To receive them, use `azure-eventhubs-source`.

Input: the body becomes the body of the event: text, bytes or a stream. A Map fails: turn it into JSON text first, for example with `json-serialize-action`. A List is sent as one event per element. The optional `partition-id` header (or `ce-partition-id`) is the partition to send to, such as `0`; without it, Event Hubs chooses one.

Output: the message is unchanged.

Good to know: the shared access policy needs the Send right.

kamelets.name: azure-eventhubs-source
kamelets.title: Azure Eventhubs Source
kamelets.summary: Receives the events of an event hub in Azure Event Hubs, one message per event, and saves how far it has read in an Azure Storage blob container.
kamelets.description:
Receives the events of an event hub in Azure Event Hubs, one message per event, and saves how far it has read in an Azure Storage blob container.

Use it to process event streams, such as telemetry or changes, that other applications send to Event Hubs. To send events, use `azure-eventhubs-sink`.

Output: the body is the body of the event, as bytes. The headers give its partition (`CamelAzureEventHubsPartitionId`), offset, sequence number and the time it was enqueued, and `CamelAzureEventHubsMetadata` holds the custom properties of the event.

Good to know: when no position has been saved yet, it starts with the events that arrive after it starts, not the older ones. It reads as the `$Default` consumer group. It saves its position (a checkpoint) in `blobContainerName` every 500 events or every 5 seconds, so after a restart some events can be read again.

kamelets.name: azure-functions-sink
kamelets.title: Azure Function Sink
kamelets.summary: Calls a function in Azure Functions over HTTP for each message, with the message as the body of the request.
kamelets.description:
Calls a function in Azure Functions over HTTP for each message, with the message as the body of the request.

Use it to run your own serverless code on each message, such as an enrichment, a notification or a calculation. For any other web service, use `http-sink`.

Input: the body is sent as the request body, as text, bytes or a stream. Turn structured data such as a Map into JSON text first, for example with `json-serialize-action`. The `Content-Type` header is sent as the content type of the request, and the other headers of the message, except the Camel ones, are sent as HTTP headers.

Output: when it is used inside a route, the body afterwards is the response of the function, and the `CamelHttpResponseCode` header its status code.

Good to know: a response with a status code outside 200 to 299 fails the message. The `key` is sent as the `code` query parameter of the request.

kamelets.name: azure-servicebus-sink
kamelets.title: Azure Servicebus Sink
kamelets.summary: Sends each message to a queue or a topic in Azure Service Bus, the Azure message broker.
kamelets.description:
Sends each message to a queue or a topic in Azure Service Bus, the Azure message broker.

Use it to hand work or events to other applications through Service Bus, such as orders to process, or notifications for all the subscribers of a topic. For simple storage queues, use `azure-storage-queue-sink`.

Input: the body is sent as text: text, bytes or a stream are read as text. A Map is sent as its text form, so turn it into JSON text first, for example with `json-serialize-action`. A List is sent as one message per element. The optional `CamelAzureServiceBusApplicationProperties` header, a Map, sets the custom properties of the message.

Output: the message is unchanged.

Good to know: the shared access policy of the connection string needs the Send right.

kamelets.name: azure-servicebus-source
kamelets.title: Azure Servicebus Source
kamelets.summary: Receives the messages of a queue, or of a topic subscription, in Azure Service Bus, one message each.
kamelets.description:
Receives the messages of a queue, or of a topic subscription, in Azure Service Bus, one message each.

Use it to process work or events that other applications send through Service Bus. To read new blobs from Event Grid events that arrive in a Service Bus queue, use `azure-storage-blob-event-based-source`.

Output: the body is the body of the Service Bus message, as bytes. The headers give its ID (`CamelAzureServiceBusMessageId`), its custom properties (`CamelAzureServiceBusApplicationProperties`, a Map), its content type, correlation ID, subject, enqueued time and delivery count.

Good to know: with the default `serviceBusReceiveMode` of `PEEK_LOCK`, a message is removed only once it has been processed; a message whose processing fails is given back and received again, until Service Bus moves it to the dead-letter queue after the maximum delivery count (10 by default). With `RECEIVE_AND_DELETE`, a message is removed as soon as it is received, so a failure loses it. For a topic, set `serviceBusType` to `topic` and `subscriptionName`.

kamelets.name: azure-storage-blob-append-sink
kamelets.title: Azure Storage Blob Append Sink
kamelets.summary: Adds each message at the end of an append blob in Azure Blob Storage, named after the `file` header, and creates the blob when it does not exist yet.
kamelets.description:
Adds each message at the end of an append blob in Azure Blob Storage, named after the `file` header, and creates the blob when it does not exist yet.

Use it to collect log lines, audit records or CSV rows from many messages into one growing blob. To write each message as a blob of its own, use `azure-storage-blob-sink`.

Input: the body is the data to add: text, bytes or a stream. It is added as it is, so end each line with a line break yourself. Turn structured data such as a Map into JSON text first, for example with `json-serialize-action`. The `file` header (or `ce-file`) is the name of the blob, such as `logs/app.log`. Without it, each message goes to a new blob with a generated unique name.

Output: the body afterwards is `true`, and headers such as `CamelAzureStorageBlobAppendOffset` and `CamelAzureStorageBlobCommittedBlockCount` describe the append.

Good to know: the container must exist: a missing container fails the message. A name that is already used by a block blob, such as one written by `azure-storage-blob-sink`, fails the message too.

kamelets.name: azure-storage-blob-changefeed-source
kamelets.title: Azure Storage Blob Changefeed Source
kamelets.summary: Reads the change feed of an Azure Storage account at a fixed interval, one message per event, such as a blob that was created or deleted.
kamelets.description:
Reads the change feed of an Azure Storage account at a fixed interval, one message per event, such as a blob that was created or deleted.

Use it to audit or replicate the changes made to the blobs of a whole storage account. To read the blobs themselves, use `azure-storage-blob-source`; to react to new blobs as they arrive, use `azure-storage-blob-event-based-source`.

Output: the body is the `data` part of the event, as JSON text. The headers `azure-storage-blob-changefeed-eventType`, `azure-storage-blob-changefeed-subject` (the path of the blob), `azure-storage-blob-changefeed-eventTime`, `azure-storage-blob-changefeed-id`, `azure-storage-blob-changefeed-topic`, `azure-storage-blob-changefeed-dataVersion` and `azure-storage-blob-changefeed-metadataVersion` give the rest of the event.

Good to know: the change feed must be turned on for the storage account (in the Azure portal: the storage account, then Data protection, then Enable blob change feed); otherwise every poll fails. It does not remember what it has read: every poll returns the whole change feed again, so the same events come again on every poll.

kamelets.name: azure-storage-blob-event-based-source
kamelets.title: Azure Storage Blob Event-based Source
kamelets.summary: Receives the Event Grid events of an Azure Storage account from a Service Bus queue and can read the content of each new blob in a container.
kamelets.description:
Receives the Event Grid events of an Azure Storage account from a Service Bus queue and can read the content of each new blob in a container.

Use it to react quickly to new blobs, such as uploaded files, without reading the container over and over. It needs an Event Grid subscription on the storage account that sends the events, in the Event Grid schema, to a Service Bus queue. To read the container on a timer instead, use `azure-storage-blob-source`.

Output: when `getBlob` is false, the default, the body is the Event Grid event as JSON (an Azure `BinaryData`, which converts to text or bytes). When `getBlob` is true, the body of a `Microsoft.Storage.BlobCreated` event for a blob of `containerName` is the content of that blob, as a stream of bytes; the other events are passed on as parsed JSON (a Jackson JSON node).

Good to know: with the default `serviceBusReceiveMode` of `RECEIVE_AND_DELETE`, an event is removed from the queue as soon as it is received, so an event whose processing fails is lost. With `getBlob`, only blobs at the top of the container can be read: an event for a blob in a virtual folder, such as `in/a.txt`, fails. It reads from a queue, not from a topic.

kamelets.name: azure-storage-blob-sink
kamelets.title: Azure Storage Blob Sink
kamelets.summary: Uploads each message as a file (a block blob) to a container in Azure Blob Storage, named after the `file` header.
kamelets.description:
Uploads each message as a file (a block blob) to a container in Azure Blob Storage, named after the `file` header.

Use it to store documents, exports or event payloads in Azure, for other applications or for archiving. To add each message at the end of one growing blob, such as a log, use `azure-storage-blob-append-sink`.

Input: the body is the content of the blob: text, bytes or a stream. Turn structured data such as a Map into JSON text first, for example with `json-serialize-action`. The optional `file` header (or `ce-file`) is the name of the blob, such as `reports/2026-05.csv`; a `/` in it puts the blob in a virtual folder. Without it, the blob gets a generated unique name.

Output: the body afterwards is `true`, and headers such as `CamelAzureStorageBlobETag` and `CamelAzureStorageBlobLastModified` describe the uploaded blob.

Good to know: a blob with the same name is replaced. The container must exist: a missing container fails the message. The name comes only from `file` or `ce-file`: to copy blobs from `azure-storage-blob-source` and keep their names, set `file` from its `CamelAzureStorageBlobBlobName` header first.

kamelets.name: azure-storage-blob-source
kamelets.title: Azure Storage Blob Source
kamelets.summary: Reads the files (blobs) in a container of Azure Blob Storage, one message per blob, and can delete each blob once it has been read.
kamelets.description:
Reads the files (blobs) in a container of Azure Blob Storage, one message per blob, and can delete each blob once it has been read.

Use it to process files that another system drops into a container, such as uploaded documents, exported reports or log files. To react to new blobs through Event Grid events instead of reading the container over and over, use `azure-storage-blob-event-based-source`.

Output: the body is the content of the blob, as a stream of bytes. The headers give the name of the blob (`CamelAzureStorageBlobBlobName`, with its folder path), its type, content type, size, ETag and last-modified time.

Good to know: blobs are kept after they are read, so the same blobs are read again on every poll, every 500 milliseconds by default; set `deleteAfterRead` to true to delete each blob once it has been processed. It reads all the blobs of the container, those in virtual folders too. With `deleteAfterRead`, the blob deleted is the one named in the `CamelAzureStorageBlobBlobName` header when processing ends, so do not change that header.

kamelets.name: azure-storage-datalake-sink
kamelets.title: Azure Storage Blob Data Lake Sink
kamelets.summary: Uploads each message as a file to a file system in Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2, named after the `file` header.
kamelets.description:
Uploads each message as a file to a file system in Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2, named after the `file` header.

Use it to land data for analytics, such as exports, events or reports, in a data lake. For plain blob containers, use `azure-storage-blob-sink`.

Input: the body is the content of the file: text, bytes or a stream. A Map fails: turn it into JSON text first, for example with `json-serialize-action`. The optional `file` header (or `ce-file`) is the name of the file, such as `sales-2026-05.csv`. Without it, the file gets a generated unique name.

Output: the body afterwards is `true`.

Good to know: by default it logs in as an app registration, with `clientId`, `clientSecret` and `tenantId`, so that app needs a role on the account that allows writing, such as Storage Blob Data Contributor.

kamelets.name: azure-storage-datalake-source
kamelets.title: Azure Storage Blob Data Lake Source
kamelets.summary: Reads the files in a file system of Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2, one message per file, on every poll.
kamelets.description:
Reads the files in a file system of Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2, one message per file, on every poll.

Use it to process files that land in a data lake, such as exports or reports. For plain blob containers, use `azure-storage-blob-source`, which can also delete what it reads.

Output: the body is the content of the file, as a stream of bytes. The `CamelAzureStorageDataLakeFileName` header is the name of the file, and other headers give its size, content type, ETag and last-modified time.

Good to know: it neither deletes nor moves the files, so it reads all of them again on every poll, every 500 milliseconds by default. It reads the files at the top of the file system: files in directories are not read.

kamelets.name: azure-storage-files-sink
kamelets.title: Azure Storage Files Sink
kamelets.summary: Uploads each message as a file to a directory of a file share in Azure Files, named after the `file` header.
kamelets.description:
Uploads each message as a file to a directory of a file share in Azure Files, named after the `file` header.

Use it to drop files where applications or people that mount the share can read them, such as reports or exports. For blob containers, use `azure-storage-blob-sink`.

Input: the body is the content of the file: text, bytes or a stream. A Map fails: turn it into JSON text first, for example with `json-serialize-action`. The optional `file` header (or `ce-file`) is the name of the file; only its last part is used, so `reports/2026/data.csv` is written as `data.csv` in `directoryName`. Without it, the file gets a generated unique name.

Output: the message is unchanged.

Good to know: a file with the same name is replaced. Missing directories are created.

kamelets.name: azure-storage-files-source
kamelets.title: Azure Storage File Source
kamelets.summary: Reads the files in a directory of a file share in Azure Files, one message per file, and can delete each file once it has been read.
kamelets.description:
Reads the files in a directory of a file share in Azure Files, one message per file, and can delete each file once it has been read.

Use it to process files that people or applications put on a share, such as scanned documents or exports. For blob containers, use `azure-storage-blob-source`.

Output: the body is the content of the file, which converts to text, bytes or a stream. The `CamelFileName` header is the path of the file from `directoryName`, `CamelFileNameOnly` its name, and `CamelFileLength` and `CamelFileLastModified` its size and last-modified time.

Good to know: files are kept after they are read, so the same files are read again on every poll, every 500 milliseconds by default; set `deleteAfterRead` to true to delete each file once it has been processed. Subdirectories are read only when `recursive` is true.

kamelets.name: azure-storage-queue-sink
kamelets.title: Azure Storage Queue Sink
kamelets.summary: Adds each message to a queue in Azure Queue Storage, as the text of a queue message.
kamelets.description:
Adds each message to a queue in Azure Queue Storage, as the text of a queue message.

Use it to hand work to another application or worker that reads the queue, such as orders to process or jobs to run. For a message broker with topics and dead-letter queues, use `azure-servicebus-sink`.

Input: the body is the text of the queue message: text or bytes. A Map is sent as its text form, so turn it into JSON text first, for example with `json-serialize-action`. The optional `expiration` header (or `ce-expiration`) sets how long the message stays in the queue, as an ISO-8601 duration such as `PT1H` (one hour) or `P2D` (two days); without it, the message expires after 7 days.

Output: the body afterwards is `true`, and headers such as `CamelAzureStorageQueueMessageId` and `CamelAzureStorageQueueExpirationTime` describe the message sent.

Good to know: the queue must exist: a missing queue fails the message. An `expiration` that is a plain number, such as `600`, fails the message.

kamelets.name: azure-storage-queue-source
kamelets.title: Azure Storage Queue Source
kamelets.summary: Receives the messages of a queue in Azure Queue Storage, one message each, and deletes each message from the queue once it has been processed.
kamelets.description:
Receives the messages of a queue in Azure Queue Storage, one message each, and deletes each message from the queue once it has been processed.

Use it to process work that other applications put in a storage queue, such as orders or jobs. For Service Bus queues and topics, use `azure-servicebus-source`.

Output: the body is the text of the queue message (as a stream). The headers give its ID (`CamelAzureStorageQueueMessageId`), the times it was inserted and expires, its pop receipt, and how many times it has been received (`CamelAzureStorageQueueDequeueCount`).

Good to know: a message whose processing fails stays in the queue and is received again 30 seconds later, with a higher dequeue count.

kamelets.name: bitcoin-source
kamelets.title: Bitcoin Source
kamelets.summary: Provides a feed of the value of the Bitcoin compared to USDT using the Binance service.
kamelets.description: Provides a feed of the value of the Bitcoin compared to USDT using the Binance service.

kamelets.name: caffeine-action
kamelets.title: Caffeine Action
kamelets.summary: Perform operations on a caffeine cache
kamelets.description: Perform operations on a caffeine cache

kamelets.name: cassandra-sink
kamelets.title: Cassandra Sink
kamelets.summary: Send data to an Apache Cassandra cluster.
kamelets.description: Send data to an Apache Cassandra cluster.

kamelets.name: cassandra-source
kamelets.title: Cassandra Source
kamelets.summary: Send a query to an Apache Cassandra cluster table.
kamelets.description: Send a query to an Apache Cassandra cluster table.

kamelets.name: ceph-event-based-source
kamelets.title: Ceph Event Based Source
kamelets.summary: Receives the bucket notifications that a Ceph Object Gateway sends to a Kafka topic, one message per event, such as a file added to or deleted from a bucket.
kamelets.description:
Receives the bucket notifications that a Ceph Object Gateway sends to a Kafka topic, one message per event, such as a file added to or deleted from a bucket.

Use it to react as soon as a file is uploaded to or removed from a Ceph bucket, without reading the bucket over and over. Set `getObject` to true to receive the content of each new file. To read and remove the files of a bucket instead, use `ceph-source`.

Output: the body is the notification as JSON text, unchanged: a `Records` array that gives the event name (such as `ObjectCreated:Put`), the bucket name and the key of the file. The headers `ceph-event-id`, `ceph-opaque-data`, `ceph-object-metadata` and `ceph-object-tags` give the fields Ceph adds to the event; metadata and tags are a List of entries with a `key` and a `val`. Each header is also set with a `ce-` name, such as `ce-cepheventid`. With `getObject` true, the body of an `ObjectCreated` event is the content of the file instead, as a stream, with its content type in `CamelAwsS3ContentType`, and the other events come out as parsed JSON (a Jackson `JsonNode`), not as text.

Good to know: the notification and its Kafka topic are set up on the Ceph side; this Kamelet only reads the topic. A record that is not a Ceph notification (without a `Records` array) fails. It connects to Kafka with no login and no TLS unless `saslAuthType` says otherwise. Without `consumerGroup`, each start uses a new group, so with the default `autoOffsetReset` of `latest` the events sent while it was stopped are not read.

kamelets.name: ceph-sink
kamelets.title: Ceph Sink
kamelets.summary: Uploads each message as a file (object) to a bucket of a Ceph Object Gateway, the S3-compatible storage of Ceph.
kamelets.description:
Uploads each message as a file (object) to a bucket of a Ceph Object Gateway, the S3-compatible storage of Ceph.

Use it to store data in Ceph, such as reports, exports, images or received messages to keep as an archive. For MinIO use `minio-sink`, and for Amazon S3 use `aws-s3-sink`.

Input: the body is the content of the file, as text, bytes or a stream. The key (the name of the file in the bucket) comes from the optional `file` header, or the `ce-file` header; when neither is set it is `keyName`, or a generated unique name when `keyName` is not set either.

Output: the body is unchanged.

Good to know: a file with the same key is overwritten, so with `keyName` set and no `file` header each message replaces the previous one. The bucket is addressed as part of the host name (such as `my-bucket.ceph.example.com`) unless `cephUrl` uses an IP address, so the gateway must accept that style of address.

kamelets.name: ceph-source
kamelets.title: Ceph Source
kamelets.summary: Reads the files (objects) in a bucket of a Ceph Object Gateway, one message per file, and by default deletes each file once it has been read.
kamelets.description:
Reads the files (objects) in a bucket of a Ceph Object Gateway, one message per file, and by default deletes each file once it has been read.

Use it to process files that another system drops into a Ceph bucket, such as uploaded documents, exported reports or log files. To react to the bucket notifications of Ceph instead of reading the bucket over and over, use `ceph-event-based-source`.

Output: the body is the content of the file, as bytes. The headers give the bucket name, the key (the path of the file in the bucket, `CamelAwsS3Key`), the content type and the ETag of the file.

Good to know: files are deleted from the bucket after they are read, unless `deleteAfterRead` is set to false; then the same files are read again on every poll. Files in folders are read too. The bucket is addressed as part of the host name (such as `my-bucket.ceph.example.com`) unless `cephUrl` uses an IP address, so the gateway must accept that style of address.

kamelets.name: chuck-norris-source
kamelets.title: Chuck Norris Source
kamelets.summary: Fetches a random Chuck Norris joke from the public api.chucknorris.io service at a regular interval, and sends it as a message.
kamelets.description:
Fetches a random Chuck Norris joke from the public api.chucknorris.io service at a regular interval, and sends it as a message.

Use it to get short, changing text messages to try out a sink, an action or a demo, with no account and no setup. For the same fixed message every time, use `timer-source`.

Output: the body is the text of one joke. The message has no headers.

Good to know: it calls `https://api.chucknorris.io` over the internet for every message, so it needs internet access.

kamelets.name: chunk-template-action
kamelets.title: Chunk Template Action
kamelets.summary: Apply a Chunk Template.
kamelets.description: Apply a Chunk Template.

kamelets.name: couchbase-sink
kamelets.title: Couchbase Sink
kamelets.summary: Send documents to Couchbase.
kamelets.description: Send documents to Couchbase.

kamelets.name: couchbase-source
kamelets.title: Couchbase Source
kamelets.summary: Poll a Couchbase bucket and emit the results.
kamelets.description: Poll a Couchbase bucket and emit the results.

kamelets.name: counter-source
kamelets.title: Counter Source
kamelets.summary: Sends a message with a number that counts up by one, such as 1, 2, 3, at a regular interval.
kamelets.description:
Sends a message with a number that counts up by one, such as 1, 2, 3, at a regular interval.

Use it to try out a sink or an action with messages that are each different and easy to follow, or to make ordered test data. For the same fixed message every time use `timer-source`, and for a calendar schedule such as "every weekday at 9:00" use `cron-source`.

Output: the body is the number, as an Integer (a whole number, not text). The `Content-Type` header is `text/plain`.

Good to know: it keeps sending until the integration is stopped, unless `numbers` is set. The count starts again from `start` when the integration restarts.

kamelets.name: cron-source
kamelets.title: Cron Source
kamelets.summary: Sends the same fixed message on a calendar schedule, written as a cron expression, such as every weekday at 9:00.
kamelets.description:
Sends the same fixed message on a calendar schedule, written as a cron expression, such as every weekday at 9:00.

Use it to start a flow at set times, such as a report every morning or a clean-up every night. For a message every few seconds or minutes, `timer-source` is simpler, and for a message that counts up use `counter-source`.

Output: the body is the `message` option as text, the same on every message. Headers about the schedule are set too, such as `fireTime` (the time of this message) and `nextFireTime`.

Good to know: the times are in the time zone of the machine it runs on. It keeps sending until the integration is stopped.

kamelets.name: crypto-decrypt-action
kamelets.title: Crypto Decrypt Action
kamelets.summary: Decrypts the body of each message that `crypto-encrypt-action` encrypted, with the same algorithm and secret key.
kamelets.description:
Decrypts the body of each message that `crypto-encrypt-action` encrypted, with the same algorithm and secret key.

Use it to get back the original data that was encrypted with `crypto-encrypt-action`, for example after reading it from storage or receiving it from another system.

Input: the encrypted data exactly as `crypto-encrypt-action` produced it, as bytes or a stream. If it was encoded on the way, for example in Base64, decode it first.

Output: the body is the original data, as bytes (a stream). The headers are kept.

Good to know: data that was changed, or a different `algorithm` or `key` than when encrypting, fails the message with "Message authentication failed". The key is a secret; keep it in a vault or a secret, not in plain configuration.

kamelets.name: crypto-encrypt-action
kamelets.title: Crypto Encrypt Action
kamelets.summary: Encrypts the body of each message with a secret key, such as an AES key, for `crypto-decrypt-action` to decrypt later with the same key.
kamelets.description:
Encrypts the body of each message with a secret key, such as an AES key, for `crypto-decrypt-action` to decrypt later with the same key.

Use it to protect sensitive data, such as personal or payment details, before it is stored or sent through a system you do not fully trust, and decrypt it later with `crypto-decrypt-action` and the same `algorithm` and `key`.

Input: text or bytes.

Output: the body is the encrypted data, as bytes (a stream), a little longer than the input. It is not text: to send it where only text fits, encode it, for example in Base64. The headers are kept.

Good to know: the key is a secret; anyone who has it can decrypt the data, so keep it in a vault or a secret, not in plain configuration. The encrypted data carries a check value, so `crypto-decrypt-action` fails on data that was changed or decrypted with another key. A key of the wrong length fails each message, not the start.

kamelets.name: data-type-action
kamelets.title: Data Type Action
kamelets.summary: Converts the body of each message into the data type you name, such as plain text, bytes, JSON, Avro or Protobuf, and sets the `Content-Type` header to match.
kamelets.description:
Converts the body of each message into the data type you name, such as plain text, bytes, JSON, Avro or Protobuf, and sets the `Content-Type` header to match.

Use it to give the next step the kind of body it needs, such as bytes for a sink that writes files, or to turn JSON into Avro binary data after `resolve-pojo-schema-action` has found the schema. A data type is a name for a kind of body together with the conversion into it; `camel catalog transformer` lists the names.

Input: `text-plain` and `application-octet-stream` take any text; `application-json` and `application-x-struct` take JSON text; `avro-binary` and `protobuf-binary` take a JSON object, as JSON text or a Jackson `JsonNode` but not a Map; `avro-x-struct` and `protobuf-x-struct` take Avro or Protobuf binary data.

Output: `text-plain` gives text (`Content-Type` `text/plain`); `application-octet-stream` bytes (`application/octet-stream`); `application-json` JSON text as bytes (`application/json`); the `x-struct` ones parsed JSON, a Jackson `JsonNode` (`application/x-struct`); `avro-binary` and `protobuf-binary` binary data (`avro/binary`, `protobuf/binary`). `application-cloudevents+json` wraps the body, under `data`, in a CloudEvents JSON envelope.

Good to know: a name that does not exist makes every message fail, and so do the Avro and Protobuf data types without a schema from an earlier `resolve-pojo-schema-action`. With `text-plain`, a Map becomes text such as `{id=1, name=Ann}`, not JSON.

kamelets.name: dns-dig-action
kamelets.title: DNS DIG Action
kamelets.summary: Asks the DNS for the records of one kind, such as A or MX, of a name, and gives the answer as text, in the format of the `dig` tool.
kamelets.description:
Asks the DNS for the records of one kind, such as A or MX, of a name, and gives the answer as text, in the format of the `dig` tool.

Use it to see the records of a domain, such as its mail (MX) records, for example to check a DNS change. To get only the IP address of a name, use `dns-ip-action`, and to get its address records as JSON, use `dns-lookup-action`.

Input: the name to look up, taken from the `domain-name` header, else from the `ce-domainname` header, else from the body as text. The kind of record comes from the `dns-type` header, else from the `ce-dnstype` header, else it is `A` (the IPv4 addresses).

Output: the body is the whole answer as text, as the `dig` command shows it: the question, the records found, and the status, such as `NOERROR`.

Good to know: a name the DNS does not know does not fail the message: the answer has the status `NXDOMAIN` and no records. The Kamelet has no options; it asks the DNS servers of the machine it runs on.

kamelets.name: dns-ip-action
kamelets.title: DNS IP Action
kamelets.summary: Finds the IP address of a host name, such as `apache.org`, and gives it as text.
kamelets.description:
Finds the IP address of a host name, such as `apache.org`, and gives it as text.

Use it to turn a host name into an address for a later step, or to check that a name can be resolved. To see all the address records of a name with how long they may be cached, use `dns-lookup-action`, and to ask for other kinds of record, such as mail (MX) records, use `dns-dig-action`.

Input: the name to look up, taken from the `domain` header, else from the `ce-domain` header, else from the body as text.

Output: the body is one IP address, as text, such as `151.101.2.132`.

Good to know: when a name has several addresses, only one of them is given. A name the DNS does not know fails the message with an unknown host error. The headers are `domain` and `ce-domain`, not `domain-name` as for `dns-lookup-action` and `dns-dig-action`. The Kamelet has no options; it uses the name resolution of the machine it runs on.

kamelets.name: dns-lookup-action
kamelets.title: DNS Lookup Action
kamelets.summary: Asks the DNS for the address records of a host name, such as `apache.org`, and gives them as JSON.
kamelets.description:
Asks the DNS for the address records of a host name, such as `apache.org`, and gives them as JSON.

Use it to check that a name exists in the DNS, or to see its records and how long they may be cached, for example to monitor a domain. To get the IP address of a name, use `dns-ip-action` instead, and to ask for other kinds of record, such as mail (MX) records, use `dns-dig-action`.

Input: the name to look up, taken from the `domain-name` header, else from the `ce-domainname` header, else from the body as text.

Output: the body is a JSON array with one entry per record found. Each entry has the type, the class and the time to live of the record.

Good to know: a name the DNS does not know fails the message with "host not found". The Kamelet has no options; it asks the DNS servers of the machine it runs on.

Before the conversion, the value of the `documentIdHeader` header is captured into the

forge its own identity in steps that read it later (the langchain4j-ingest sink does);
the body is pinned to bytes and the `CamelDocling*` control headers are swept, because
none of them may be decided by a consumer-delivered payload. By default the `docling`
component executes a local docling CLI; set `doclingServeUrl` to use a Docling Serve
instance instead - the natural fit for self-contained Pipes. With `maxDocumentSize`
set, a payload larger than that many bytes fails the exchange before the conversion.

kamelets.name: drop-field-action
kamelets.title: Drop Field Action
kamelets.summary: Removes one field, chosen by its name, from each message that is a JSON object.
kamelets.description:
Removes one field, chosen by its name, from each message that is a JSON object.

Use it to take out a field that the next system does not accept or should not see, such as an internal ID or a password. To remove several fields, or to keep only some, use `replace-field-action`; to keep the field but hide its value, use `mask-field-action`.

Input: a JSON object, as JSON text or as parsed JSON (a Map or a Jackson `JsonNode`). Only the fields at the top level of the object are looked at. A JSON array is passed on unchanged; a body that is not JSON fails.

Output: the same object without the field. When the `Content-Type` header is `application/json`, the body is JSON text again; otherwise it is parsed JSON (a Jackson `JsonNode`), which `json-serialize-action` turns into JSON text.

Good to know: a message without the field is passed on unchanged. A field of the same name inside a nested object is not removed.

kamelets.name: drop-header-action
kamelets.title: Drop Header Action
kamelets.summary: Removes one header, given by its name, from each message.
kamelets.description:
Removes one header, given by its name, from each message.

Use it to remove a header that the next step must not see, for example an `Authorization` header with a secret, or a header that would change what a sink does. To remove several headers at once by a pattern, such as all the headers whose names start with `Camel`, use `drop-headers-action`.

Input: any message.

Output: the same body, and the same headers without the one named by `name`. A message without that header passes on unchanged.

Good to know: the name is not case-sensitive: `FOO` also removes the header `foo`.

kamelets.name: drop-headers-action
kamelets.title: Drop Headers Action
kamelets.summary: Removes from each message all the headers whose names match a pattern, such as `Camel*`.
kamelets.description:
Removes from each message all the headers whose names match a pattern, such as `Camel*`.

Use it to remove the internal `Camel*` headers that came with a message from outside before it reaches a sink, or to clear many headers at once before a message goes to another system. To remove a single header by its name, `drop-header-action` is enough.

Input: any message.

Output: the same body, without the headers that match `pattern`. The headers that match `excludePattern` are kept.

Good to know: a pattern is compared with each header name first as an exact name, then as a wildcard when it ends with `*` (`x-*` matches every name that starts with `x-`), and then as a Java regular expression, such as `x-(one|two)`. None of these comparisons is case-sensitive.

Use it to follow the earthquakes around the world, for example to alert on the strong ones, or as a stream of real, changing JSON data for a demo. No account is needed.

Good to know: the first check sends the earthquakes whose report was updated in the last `lookAhead` minutes, and each later check those updated since the check before. An earthquake is sent again when USGS updates its report. The time of the last check is kept in memory only, so a restart begins again with the last `lookAhead` minutes. It calls `https://earthquake.usgs.gov` over the internet.

kamelets.name: file-watch-source
kamelets.title: File Watch Source
kamelets.summary: Sends a message each time a file in a local directory is created, changed or deleted, with the kind of change and the path of the file.
kamelets.description:
Sends a message each time a file in a local directory is created, changed or deleted, with the kind of change and the path of the file.

Use it to react to files that another program writes into a directory on the same machine, for example to start processing when a new export appears, or to keep track of the changes in a folder. To read files from a remote server instead, use `ftp-source`, `sftp-source` or `aws-s3-source`.

Output: the body is the file that changed, which the next step can read as text or bytes; a deleted file or a directory has no content to read. The `CamelFileEventType` header is `CREATE`, `MODIFY` or `DELETE`, `CamelFileName` is the path of the file relative to the watched directory, and `CamelFileAbsolutePath` is its full path.

Good to know: it watches the subdirectories too, new ones included. It never changes or deletes the files. Only changes made while it runs are sent, not the files that are already there when it starts. The path must be a directory, not a single file; it is created when it does not exist. kamelets.name: freemarker-template-action
kamelets.title: Freemarker Template Action
kamelets.summary: Builds a new message body from a FreeMarker template, filling in values from the incoming message.
kamelets.description:
Builds a new message body from a FreeMarker template, filling in values from the incoming message.

Use it to turn data into text for people or for another system, such as an email, a report or a small XML or JSON document, when you already have FreeMarker templates or need its loops and conditions. For simple templates, `mustache-template-action` is an alternative; to reshape JSON into other JSON, `jslt-action` is often simpler.

Input: any body. The template sees the body as `$\{body}` and a header as `${headers.name}`, for example `Dear ${headers.customer}, your order $\{body} has shipped.`

Output: the body is the text the template produced. The headers are kept.

Good to know: a value the template uses that is missing, such as a header that is not set, fails the message; give a default with `${headers.customer!""}`. A template file that cannot be found fails the message too. The template is loaded from a file, the classpath or a URL given by the `template` option; it cannot come from the message.

kamelets.name: ftp-sink
kamelets.title: FTP Sink
kamelets.summary: Uploads each message as a file to a directory on an FTP server.
kamelets.description:
Uploads each message as a file to a directory on an FTP server.

Use it to deliver exports, reports or data files to a partner or a legacy system that receives files over FTP. For an encrypted connection use `ftps-sink`, and for a server you reach with SSH use `sftp-sink`.

Input: the body is the content of the file, as text, bytes or a stream. The name of the file comes from the `file` header, or from `ce-file` when `file` is not set; any directory in it is dropped, so `reports/data.csv` is written as `data.csv`. Without these headers, `CamelFileName` is used as it is, subdirectories included, and without any of them a unique name is generated.

Output: the message is unchanged. The `CamelFileNameProduced` header is set to the path of the file on the server.

Good to know: a file with the same name is replaced, unless `fileExist` says otherwise. The connection and the login are not encrypted. A file name that points outside `directoryName` fails the message. Files are sent in ASCII (text) mode unless `binary` is true.

kamelets.name: ftp-source
kamelets.title: FTP Source
kamelets.summary: Reads the files in a directory on an FTP server, one message per file, and by default leaves them on the server.
kamelets.description:
Reads the files in a directory on an FTP server, one message per file, and by default leaves them on the server.

Use it to collect the files that a partner or a legacy system drops on an FTP server, such as orders, invoices or exports. For an encrypted connection use `ftps-source`, and for a server you reach with SSH use `sftp-source`.

Output: the body is the content of the file, as a stream. The `file` and `ce-file` headers hold the name of the file, with its path below `directoryName` when `recursive` is true, such as `2026/orders.csv`. `CamelFileName` holds the same name, and `CamelFileLength` the size of the file in bytes.

Good to know: files are not deleted or moved after they are read, unless `delete` is true. A file is read only once while the integration runs (`idempotent`), but the files left on the server are all read again after a restart; set `delete` to true to read each file only once. The connection and the login are not encrypted. Files are transferred in ASCII (text) mode unless `binary` is true.

kamelets.name: ftps-sink
kamelets.title: FTPS Sink
kamelets.summary: Uploads each message as a file to a directory on an FTPS server, which is FTP with TLS encryption.
kamelets.description:
Uploads each message as a file to a directory on an FTPS server, which is FTP with TLS encryption.

Use it to deliver exports, reports or data files to a partner or a legacy system that receives files over FTPS. For a server without TLS use `ftp-sink`, and for a server you reach with SSH use `sftp-sink`.

Input: the body is the content of the file, as text, bytes or a stream. The name of the file comes from the `file` header, or from `ce-file` when `file` is not set; any directory in it is dropped, so `reports/data.csv` is written as `data.csv`. Without these headers, `CamelFileName` is used as it is, subdirectories included, and without any of them a unique name is generated.

Output: the message is unchanged. The `CamelFileNameProduced` header is set to the path of the file on the server.

Good to know: a file with the same name is replaced, unless `fileExist` says otherwise. It uses explicit TLS: it connects to the normal FTP port, usually 21, and then switches to TLS. A server that only accepts implicit TLS, usually on port 990, is not supported. A file name that points outside `directoryName` fails the message. Files are sent in ASCII (text) mode unless `binary` is true.

kamelets.name: ftps-source
kamelets.title: FTPS Source
kamelets.summary: Reads the files in a directory on an FTPS server (FTP with TLS encryption), one message per file, and by default leaves them on the server.
kamelets.description:
Reads the files in a directory on an FTPS server (FTP with TLS encryption), one message per file, and by default leaves them on the server.

Use it to collect the files that a partner or a legacy system drops on an FTPS server, such as orders, invoices or exports. For a server without TLS use `ftp-source`, and for a server you reach with SSH use `sftp-source`.

Output: the body is the content of the file, as a stream. The `file` and `ce-file` headers hold the name of the file, with its path below `directoryName` when `recursive` is true, such as `2026/orders.csv`. `CamelFileName` holds the same name, and `CamelFileLength` the size of the file in bytes.

Good to know: files are not deleted or moved after they are read, unless `delete` is true. A file is read only once while the integration runs (`idempotent`), but the files left on the server are all read again after a restart; set `delete` to true to read each file only once. It uses explicit TLS: it connects to the normal FTP port, usually 21, and then switches to TLS. A server that only accepts implicit TLS, usually on port 990, is not supported. Files are transferred in ASCII (text) mode unless `binary` is true.

kamelets.name: github-commit-source
kamelets.title: GitHub Commit Source
kamelets.summary: Receives each new commit on a branch of a GitHub repository, one message per commit, oldest first, by asking the GitHub API for new commits.
kamelets.description:
Receives each new commit on a branch of a GitHub repository, one message per commit, oldest first, by asking the GitHub API for new commits.

Use it to start a flow when code is pushed, for example to post the commit message to a chat channel or to trigger a build or a deployment.

Output: the body is the commit message as JSON text, that is a quoted JSON string such as `"Fix the login page"`. The `CamelGitHubCommitSha` header gives the SHA of the commit, `CamelGitHubCommitUrl` its web address, and `CamelGitHubCommitAuthor` and `CamelGitHubCommitCommitter` the names of its author and committer.

Good to know: with the default `startingSha` of `last`, only the commits made after the start are sent. It works with github.com, not with GitHub Enterprise Server. It asks GitHub for new commits about twice a second, and every request counts against the API rate limit of the token.

kamelets.name: github-event-source
kamelets.title: GitHub Event Source
kamelets.summary: Receives the activity of a GitHub repository, such as pushes, issues, pull requests and stars, one message per event, by asking the GitHub API for new events.
kamelets.description:
Receives the activity of a GitHub repository, such as pushes, issues, pull requests and stars, one message per event, by asking the GitHub API for new events.

Use it to follow everything that happens in a repository in one flow, for example to log it or to count it. To receive only commits, pull requests, comments on pull requests or tags, use `github-commit-source`, `github-pullrequest-source`, `github-pullrequest-comment-source` or `github-tag-source`.

Output: the body is the type of the event as JSON text, that is a quoted JSON string such as `"PUSH"`, `"PULL_REQUEST"` or `"ISSUES"`. The details of the event are only in the `CamelGitHubEventPayload` header, as a Java object.

Good to know: when it starts, it first sends the recent events that GitHub still lists for the repository, not only the new ones. It works with github.com, not with GitHub Enterprise Server. It asks GitHub for new events about twice a second, and every request counts against the API rate limit of the token.

kamelets.name: github-pullrequest-comment-source
kamelets.title: GitHub Pull Request Comments Source
kamelets.summary: Receives each new comment written on the open pull requests of a GitHub repository, one message per comment, by asking the GitHub API for new comments.
kamelets.description:
Receives each new comment written on the open pull requests of a GitHub repository, one message per comment, by asking the GitHub API for new comments.

Use it to react to the discussion on pull requests, for example to answer a command written in a comment, such as `/retest`, or to forward the comments to a chat channel. To receive the pull requests themselves, use `github-pullrequest-source`.

Output: the body is the comment as JSON text. The `CamelGitHubPullRequest` header gives the number of the pull request it was written on.

Good to know: only the comments written after the start are sent, and only on pull requests that are still open. These are the comments of the conversation of a pull request, not the review comments on lines of code. It works with github.com, not with GitHub Enterprise Server. About twice a second it asks GitHub for the open pull requests and for the comments of each of them, and every request counts against the API rate limit of the token.

kamelets.name: github-pullrequest-source
kamelets.title: GitHub Pull Request Source
kamelets.summary: Receives each new pull request opened in a GitHub repository, one message per pull request, by asking the GitHub API for new open pull requests.
kamelets.description:
Receives each new pull request opened in a GitHub repository, one message per pull request, by asking the GitHub API for new open pull requests.

Use it to react when someone proposes a change, for example to announce the pull request in a chat channel, open a review ticket or start a check. To receive the comments on pull requests, use `github-pullrequest-comment-source`.

Output: the body is the pull request as JSON text. The `CamelGitHubPullRequest` header gives its number, and `CamelGitHubPullRequestHeadCommitSha` the SHA of its latest commit.

Good to know: only the pull requests opened after the start are sent, once each; updates, merges and closes are not. It works with github.com, not with GitHub Enterprise Server. It asks GitHub for new pull requests about twice a second, and every request counts against the API rate limit of the token.

kamelets.name: github-tag-source
kamelets.title: GitHub Tag Source
kamelets.summary: Receives each new tag created in a GitHub repository, one message per tag, by asking the GitHub API for the tags of the repository.
kamelets.description:
Receives each new tag created in a GitHub repository, one message per tag, by asking the GitHub API for the tags of the repository.

Use it to react to a new version, for example to announce a release, update a changelog or start a deployment. To receive every commit instead, use `github-commit-source`.

Output: the body is the tag as JSON text.

Good to know: only the tags created after the start are sent; the tags that exist when it starts are skipped. It works with github.com, not with GitHub Enterprise Server. It asks GitHub for the tags about twice a second, and every request counts against the API rate limit of the token.
