kamelets.name: has-header-filter-action
kamelets.title: Has Header Filter Action
kamelets.summary: Keeps only the messages that have a given header, optionally with a given value, and drops all others.
kamelets.description:
Keeps only the messages that have a given header, optionally with a given value, and drops all others.

Use it to pass on only the messages that carry a marker, such as a `priority` header, or only those of one kind, such as the events whose `type` header is `order`. To match the value of a header against a pattern, use `header-matches-filter-action`, and to keep or drop messages by the content of a JSON body, use `predicate-filter-action`.

Input: any message. The header named by `name` is read.

Output: the same message, unchanged, when it has the header and, when `value` is set, when the header has exactly that value. Otherwise the message is dropped and nothing is sent on.

Good to know: the comparison with `value` is case-sensitive: `order` does not match `Order`. A header with an empty value counts as present when `value` is not set.

kamelets.name: header-matches-filter-action
kamelets.title: Header Matches Filter Action
kamelets.summary: Keeps only the messages whose value of a given header matches a regular expression, and drops all others.
kamelets.description:
Keeps only the messages whose value of a given header matches a regular expression, and drops all others.

Use it to pass on only some messages, for example only the events whose `type` header has the form `order-` followed by a number, or only the messages of some customers by a `customerId` header. To check only that a header is there, or has one exact value, `has-header-filter-action` is simpler, and to filter Kafka records by their topic, use `topic-name-matches-filter-action`.

Input: any message. The header named by `headerName` is read.

Output: the same message, unchanged, when the value of the header matches `regex`. Otherwise, and when the message does not have the header, the message is dropped and nothing is sent on.

Good to know: the expression must match the whole value, not only a part of it: `order-[0-9]+` matches `order-1` but not `x-order-1`, and it is case-sensitive. `headerName` must be set: the Kamelet does not start without it.

kamelets.name: hoist-field-action
kamelets.title: Hoist Field Action
kamelets.summary: Wraps the body of each message in a new JSON object, as the value of the one field you name.
kamelets.description:
Wraps the body of each message in a new JSON object, as the value of the one field you name.

Use it to nest the whole message under one name, for example to turn `{"id":1}` into `{"order":{"id":1}}` for a system that expects that shape. To do the opposite, and take the value out of a field, use `extract-field-action`.

Input: any body. JSON is nested as a JSON object or array when it is parsed JSON (a Map or a Jackson `JsonNode`), or JSON text with the `Content-Type` header `application/json`. Any other text, including JSON text with another `Content-Type`, becomes a text value: `hello` gives `{"order":"hello"}`.

Output: the body is the new JSON object, as JSON text, and the `Content-Type` header is set to `application/json`.

kamelets.name: http-secured-sink
kamelets.title: Secured HTTP Sink
kamelets.summary: Sends each message to a web service or REST API as an HTTP or HTTPS request, logging in with a user and password or with an OAuth 2.0 token.
kamelets.description:
Sends each message to a web service or REST API as an HTTP or HTTPS request, logging in with a user and password or with an OAuth 2.0 token.

Use it to push data to a service that needs a login, such as a protected webhook, an internal REST API, or an API that gives out OAuth 2.0 tokens to applications. If the service needs no login, use `http-sink` instead.

Input: the body is sent as the request body, as text, bytes or a stream. Turn structured data such as a Map into JSON text first, for example with `json-serialize-action`. The `Content-Type` header is sent as the content type of the request, and the other headers of the message, except the Camel ones, are sent as HTTP headers.

Output: when it is used inside a route, the body afterwards is the response of the service.

Good to know: a response with a status code of 300 or higher fails the message. The address and the method come only from the options; headers on the message cannot change where it is sent. Log in either with `authUsername` and `authPassword`, or with `oauth2ClientId`, `oauth2ClientSecret` and `oauth2TokenEndpoint`: the Kamelet then gets a token from that URL and sends it as a Bearer token. Without `authenticationPreemptive`, the user and password are sent only after the service asks for them with a 401 response.

kamelets.name: http-secured-source
kamelets.title: HTTP Secured Source
kamelets.summary: Fetches a web address with an HTTP GET request at a regular interval, logging in with a user and password or with an OAuth 2.0 token, and sends each response as a message.
kamelets.description:
Fetches a web address with an HTTP GET request at a regular interval, logging in with a user and password or with an OAuth 2.0 token, and sends each response as a message.

Use it to poll a protected REST API or feed for its current data, for example fetch the state of the orders every minute. If the address needs no login, use `http-source`. To receive the requests that other systems send instead, use `webhook-source`.

Output: the body is the body of the response, as bytes. The headers of the response, such as `Content-Type`, are copied to the message, and `CamelHttpResponseCode` holds the status code.

Good to know: it fetches the address every `period` and sends a message for each response, even when the data has not changed. A response with a status code of 300 or higher sends no message: the error is logged, and the address is fetched again at the next period. Log in either with `authUsername` and `authPassword`, or with `oauth2ClientId`, `oauth2ClientSecret` and `oauth2TokenEndpoint`: the Kamelet then gets a token from that URL and sends it as a Bearer token.

kamelets.name: http-sink
kamelets.title: HTTP Sink
kamelets.summary: Sends each message to a web service or REST API as an HTTP or HTTPS request, for example a POST of JSON to a webhook.
kamelets.description:
Sends each message to a web service or REST API as an HTTP or HTTPS request, for example a POST of JSON to a webhook.

Use it to push data to any service that accepts HTTP calls, such as a webhook, a REST API or a serverless function. If the service needs a login (Basic or OAuth), use `http-secured-sink` instead.

Input: the body is sent as the request body, as text, bytes or a stream. Turn structured data such as a Map into JSON text first, for example with `json-serialize-action`. The `Content-Type` header is sent as the content type of the request, and the other headers of the message, except the Camel ones, are sent as HTTP headers.

Output: when it is used inside a route, the body afterwards is the response of the service.

Good to know: a response with a status code of 300 or higher fails the message. The address and the method come only from the options; headers on the message cannot change where it is sent.

kamelets.name: http-source
kamelets.title: HTTP Source
kamelets.summary: Fetches a web address with an HTTP GET request at a regular interval, and sends each response as a message.
kamelets.description:
Fetches a web address with an HTTP GET request at a regular interval, and sends each response as a message.

Use it to poll a REST API, a feed or a status page for its current data, for example fetch the state of the orders every minute. If the address needs a login, use `http-secured-source`. To receive the requests that other systems send instead, use `webhook-source`.

Output: the body is the body of the response, as bytes. The headers of the response, such as `Content-Type`, are copied to the message, and `CamelHttpResponseCode` holds the status code.

Good to know: it fetches the address every `period` and sends a message for each response, even when the data has not changed. A response with a status code of 300 or higher sends no message: the error is logged, and the address is fetched again at the next period.

kamelets.name: insert-field-action
kamelets.title: Insert Field Action
kamelets.summary: Adds a field with a value you choose to each message that is a JSON object, or replaces the value when the field is already there.
kamelets.description:
Adds a field with a value you choose to each message that is a JSON object, or replaces the value when the field is already there.

Use it to tag records with where they come from or which environment they passed through, or to add a value from a header or the current date. To add a header instead of a field, use `insert-header-action`.

Input: a JSON object, as JSON text or as parsed JSON (a Map or a Jackson `JsonNode`). When the body is a JSON array, the value is added at the end of the array and `field` is not used. A body that is not JSON fails.

Output: the object with the field. When the `Content-Type` header is `application/json`, the body is JSON text again; otherwise it is parsed JSON (a Jackson `JsonNode`), which `json-serialize-action` turns into JSON text.

Good to know: the value is always added as a JSON text value, in quotes, even when it looks like a number. The field is added at the top level of the object.

kamelets.name: insert-header-action
kamelets.title: Insert Header Action
kamelets.summary: Adds a header to each message, or replaces it, with a fixed text or a value taken from the message.
kamelets.description:
Adds a header to each message, or replaces it, with a fixed text or a value taken from the message.

Use it to give a sink the headers it reads, such as the `ce-projectKey` header of `jira-add-issue-sink`, to tag messages with where they come from, or to copy the body into a header for a later step. To set the key of a Kafka record, `set-kafka-key-action` is simpler.

Input: any message.

Output: the same body. The header named by `name` is set to `value`, and replaces a header of the same name.

Good to know: `value` is written in the Camel Simple language: plain text is used as it is, and the `${...}` parts are filled in from the message, such as `$\{body}` for the body, or `${header.source}` for the value of the header `source`.

kamelets.name: is-tombstone-filter-action
kamelets.title: Is Tombstone Filter Action
kamelets.summary: Drops the Kafka records that have no value, called tombstones, and passes on all other messages unchanged.
kamelets.description:
Drops the Kafka records that have no value, called tombstones, and passes on all other messages unchanged.

Use it to skip tombstones, which mark a key as deleted in a compacted topic, after `kafka-source` when the next step cannot handle a message without a body.

Input: any message.

Output: the same message, unchanged, when it has a body. A message with no body, or with empty text as its body, is dropped and nothing is sent on.

kamelets.name: jira-add-comment-sink
kamelets.title: Jira Add Comment Sink
kamelets.summary: Adds the text of each message as a new comment to an existing issue in Jira.
kamelets.description:
Adds the text of each message as a new comment to an existing issue in Jira.

Use it to record on a ticket what happened elsewhere, for example a deployment, the result of a build or a reply of a customer. To create issues use `jira-add-issue-sink`, to change their fields `jira-update-issue-sink`, and to change their status `jira-transition-issue-sink`.

Input: the body is the text of the comment, as text. The `ce-issueKey` header, the key of the issue such as `SHOP-42`, is required. Set it before this sink, for example with `insert-header-action`.

Output: the message is unchanged.

Good to know: a message without `ce-issueKey`, or for an issue that does not exist or that the user cannot see, fails. The comment is written in the name of the account the Kamelet logs in with. Log in either with `username` and `password`, or with `personal-token`.

kamelets.name: jira-add-issue-sink
kamelets.title: Jira Add Issue Sink
kamelets.summary: Creates a new issue, such as a bug or a task, in a Jira project for each message.
kamelets.description:
Creates a new issue, such as a bug or a task, in a Jira project for each message.

Use it to open a ticket automatically when something happens, for example when a monitoring alert fires, a form is submitted or an order fails.

Input: the body is the description of the issue, as text. The other fields come from headers. `ce-projectKey` (the key of the project, such as `SHOP`), `ce-issueTypeName` (such as `Bug` or `Task`) and `ce-issueSummary` (the title) are required. `ce-issueAssignee`, `ce-issuePriorityName` (such as `High`) and `ce-issueComponents` (a comma-separated list) are optional. Set them before this sink, for example with `insert-header-action`.

Output: when it is used inside a route, the body afterwards is the issue that was created.

Good to know: a message without a project key, an issue type or a summary fails. Log in either with `username` and `password`, or with `personal-token`.

kamelets.name: jira-oauth-source
kamelets.title: Jira oauth Source
kamelets.summary: Receives each new Jira issue that matches a JQL query, such as every new bug of a project, by asking Jira at a regular interval, and logs in with OAuth 1.0a.
kamelets.description:
Receives each new Jira issue that matches a JQL query, such as every new bug of a project, by asking Jira at a regular interval, and logs in with OAuth 1.0a.

Use it to react to new tickets of a Jira Server or Data Center where an administrator has set up an application link with OAuth for your integration, for example to tell a team chat about a new bug. To log in with a user and an API token or a personal access token, which is simpler, use `jira-source`.

Output: the body is the issue as JSON text, with fields such as `key`, `summary`, `description`, `status`, `issueType`, `project`, `reporter`, `assignee` and `priority`.

Good to know: only the issues created after the Kamelet starts are sent; the issues that already exist are not, and neither are changes to an issue. It checks every 6 seconds. The four OAuth values come from the OAuth 1.0a authorization of the application link, see each option.

kamelets.name: jira-source
kamelets.title: Jira Source
kamelets.summary: Receives each new Jira issue that matches a JQL query, such as every new bug of a project, by asking Jira at a regular interval.
kamelets.description:
Receives each new Jira issue that matches a JQL query, such as every new bug of a project, by asking Jira at a regular interval.

Use it to react when a ticket is opened, for example to tell a team chat about a new bug or to copy new issues into another tracker. To log in with OAuth 1.0a instead of a password or a token, use `jira-oauth-source`.

Output: the body is the issue as JSON text, with fields such as `key`, `summary`, `description`, `status`, `issueType`, `project`, `reporter`, `assignee` and `priority`.

Good to know: only the issues created after the Kamelet starts are sent; the issues that already exist are not, and neither are changes to an issue. It checks every 6 seconds. `jql` must be set, or the Kamelet does not start. Log in either with `username` and `password`, or with `personal-token`.

kamelets.name: jira-transition-issue-sink
kamelets.title: Jira Transition Issue Sink
kamelets.summary: Moves an existing Jira issue to another status, such as from `In Progress` to `Done`, by running a transition of its workflow for each message.
kamelets.description:
Moves an existing Jira issue to another status, such as from `In Progress` to `Done`, by running a transition of its workflow for each message.

Use it to keep tickets in step with what happens elsewhere, for example to close an issue when its fix is deployed or to reopen it when a test fails again. To change other fields use `jira-update-issue-sink`, and to only add a comment `jira-add-comment-sink`.

Input: the `ce-issueKey` header (the key of the issue, such as `SHOP-42`) and the `ce-issueTransitionId` header (the ID number of the transition, such as `31`, not the name of the status) are required. The body, as text, is added to the issue as a comment after the transition.

Output: the message is unchanged.

Good to know: a message without one of the two headers fails, and so does a transition that the workflow does not allow from the current status of the issue. Jira lists the transitions possible for an issue, with their IDs, at `<jiraUrl>/rest/api/2/issue/<key>/transitions`. Log in either with `username` and `password`, or with `personal-token`.

kamelets.name: jira-update-issue-sink
kamelets.title: Jira Update Issue Sink
kamelets.summary: Changes the fields of an existing Jira issue, such as its summary, description, assignee or priority, for each message.
kamelets.description:
Changes the fields of an existing Jira issue, such as its summary, description, assignee or priority, for each message.

Use it to keep a ticket in step with another system, for example to assign an issue to the person on call or to raise its priority when an alert repeats. To change the status use `jira-transition-issue-sink`, and to create issues `jira-add-issue-sink`.

Input: the body becomes the new description of the issue, as text, and replaces the old one. The `ce-issueKey` header (the key of the issue, such as `SHOP-42`) is required. The other fields come from optional headers, and a field without a header is left as it is: `ce-issueSummary` (the title), `ce-issueTypeName` (such as `Bug`), `ce-issueAssignee`, `ce-issuePriorityName` (such as `High`) and `ce-issueComponents` (a comma-separated list, which replaces the components).

Output: the message is unchanged.

Good to know: every message replaces the description with its body; the `ce-issueDescription` header is not used. An issue type or a priority whose name Jira does not know is ignored. A message without `ce-issueKey` fails. Log in either with `username` and `password`, or with `personal-token`.

kamelets.name: jolt-transformation-action
kamelets.title: Jolt Transformation Action
kamelets.summary: Reshapes each JSON message into other JSON, as a Jolt specification describes: moves, renames, removes fields or adds defaults.
kamelets.description:
Reshapes each JSON message into other JSON, as a Jolt specification describes: moves, renames, removes fields or adds defaults.

Use it to map the JSON of one system to the JSON another system expects, for example to rename fields or move them into a nested object, when you already have Jolt specifications. `jslt-action` does the same with a query language, and is often easier to write.

Input: parsed JSON, a Map (or a List). Since Camel 4.24, JSON text, bytes and a stream work too. With older versions they do not fail but give an empty body, and so does the parsed JSON of `json-deserialize-action`.

Output: the body is the result as parsed JSON, a Map (or a List), not JSON text. Add `json-serialize-action` after it to get JSON text. The headers are kept.

Good to know: the specification cannot read headers, only the body. It is loaded from a file, the classpath or a URL given by the `template` option; it cannot come from the message.

kamelets.name: jslt-action
kamelets.title: JSLT Action
kamelets.summary: Turns each JSON message into new JSON with a JSLT transformation, a query language for JSON that picks, renames and computes fields.
kamelets.description:
Turns each JSON message into new JSON with a JSLT transformation, a query language for JSON that picks, renames and computes fields.

Use it to map the JSON of one system to the JSON another system expects, for example to keep only some fields, rename them or count the items of an order. To build text rather than JSON, use `mustache-template-action`; `jolt-transformation-action` reshapes JSON with Jolt specifications instead.

Input: JSON text, bytes or a stream. The transformation sees the body as `.` and a header as `$headers.name`, for example `{"customer": .name, "items": size(.items), "source": $headers.origin}`.

Output: the body is the result as JSON text. The headers are kept.

Good to know: parsed JSON (a Map or a JsonNode, such as the output of `json-deserialize-action`) fails the message: give the JSON as text. A field whose value is missing, such as a header that is not set, is left out of the result. The transformation is loaded from a file, the classpath or a URL given by the `template` option; it cannot come from the message.

kamelets.name: json-deserialize-action
kamelets.title: Json Deserialize Action
kamelets.summary: Turns a body of JSON text into parsed JSON, a Jackson `JsonNode`, so that the next steps can work with its fields.
kamelets.description:
Turns a body of JSON text into parsed JSON, a Jackson `JsonNode`, so that the next steps can work with its fields.

Use it to prepare a message for a step that needs parsed JSON rather than text, such as `jsonata-action`, or to make sure that a body is well-formed JSON. To turn parsed data back into JSON text, use `json-serialize-action`, and to check JSON against a schema, use `json-schema-validator-action`.

Input: JSON text, as text or bytes: a JSON object or a JSON array.

Output: the body is parsed JSON, a Jackson `JsonNode`: an object node for a JSON object, an array node for a JSON array. The `Content-Type` header is removed.

Good to know: a body that is not valid JSON fails the message.

kamelets.name: json-schema-validator-action
kamelets.title: Json Schema Validator Action
kamelets.summary: Checks that each JSON message matches a JSON Schema, and fails the messages that do not.
kamelets.description:
Checks that each JSON message matches a JSON Schema, and fails the messages that do not.

Use it to stop bad data early, for example to reject the orders that miss a required field before they reach a database or another system. To keep or drop messages by a condition instead of failing them, use `predicate-filter-action`.

Input: JSON text, as text, bytes or a stream, or parsed JSON from `json-deserialize-action`. A Map fails.

Output: the same message, unchanged, when it matches the schema.

Good to know: a message that does not match the schema, or that is not JSON, fails with an error that lists what is wrong; it is not dropped silently, so the error handling of the integration decides what happens to it. The schema is loaded from the `template` location; it cannot come from the message.

kamelets.name: json-serialize-action
kamelets.title: Json Serialize Action
kamelets.summary: Turns a body of parsed data, such as a Map, a List or parsed JSON, into JSON text.
kamelets.description:
Turns a body of parsed data, such as a Map, a List or parsed JSON, into JSON text.

Use it to send parsed data to a sink that needs JSON text, for example after `jsonata-action` or `json-deserialize-action`, whose output is parsed JSON. To do the opposite, use `json-deserialize-action`.

Input: parsed data: a Map, a List, or parsed JSON (a Jackson `JsonNode`).

Output: the body is JSON text, as a stream of bytes. The `Content-Type` header is set to `application/json`.

Good to know: a body that is already text becomes one JSON string, in quotes: `hello` becomes `"hello"`, and JSON text is quoted the same way. Do not use it on a body that is already JSON text.

kamelets.name: jsonata-action
kamelets.title: Jsonata Action
kamelets.summary: Transforms each JSON message with a JSONata expression, to reshape it, pick out fields, or compute new values.
kamelets.description:
Transforms each JSON message with a JSONata expression, to reshape it, pick out fields, or compute new values.

Use it to turn the JSON of one system into the JSON another system expects, for example to rename fields, join a first and a last name, or add up the lines of an order. For other ways to reshape JSON, see `jslt-action` and `jolt-transformation-action`; to build text, such as an email, from a template, use `mustache-template-action`.

Input: parsed JSON, such as a Map, a List, or the output of `json-deserialize-action`.

Output: the body is the result of the expression, as parsed JSON (a Jackson `JsonNode`), not as text: add `json-serialize-action` after it to get JSON text. The headers are kept.

Good to know: put `json-deserialize-action` before it when the body is JSON text, as depending on the Camel version the expression sees JSON text as one string rather than as an object, and bytes or a stream fail. The expression is loaded from the `template` location; it cannot come from the message.

kamelets.name: kafka-apicurio-registry-not-secured-sink
kamelets.title: Kafka Not Secured with Apicurio Registry Sink
kamelets.summary: Sends each message as an Avro record to a topic in Apache Kafka, with the schema kept in an Apicurio Registry, and no login or TLS to either.
kamelets.description:
Sends each message as an Avro record to a topic in Apache Kafka, with the schema kept in an Apicurio Registry, and no login or TLS to either.

kamelets.title: LangChain4j Ingest File Source
kamelets.summary: Watch a directory as the source of an ingestion pipeline, with the defaults a knowledge base needs.
kamelets.description:
Watch a directory as the source of an ingestion pipeline, with the defaults a knowledge
base needs.

The defaults: documents are left in place (noop), unchanged files are remembered in a
duplicate register keyed on path, modification time and size, a file still being copied
in is waited for (readLock=changed), and the file name is exposed as the document id in
the CamelLangChain4jIngestDocumentId header.

Mind the two dedup layers when composing: this source re-delivers an edited file (its
register key changes with the modification time), but a langchain4j-ingest-sink with an
idempotentRepository is first-write-wins by document id - the re-delivered edit would
be skipped. Use a version-aware id, or no sink repository, when documents change.

kamelets.name: langchain4j-ingest-sink

kamelets.summary: Ingest documents into a LangChain4j EmbeddingStore.
kamelets.description:
Ingest documents into a LangChain4j EmbeddingStore.

The payload is split into overlapping segments, embedded in batches and written to the
store, each segment stamped with the pipeline name and the document id.

The document id is read from the `CamelLangChain4jIngestDocumentId` exchange property
when a prior step captured it (the parser actions do, before the parse), else from the
header named by `documentIdHeader` - the property always wins, so a parsed document
cannot forge its own identity. Bean references are `#bean:name` values; when
`embeddingStore` or `embeddingModel` is not set, the single registry bean of that type is
used. With `idempotentRepository` set, the first write per document id wins - a
re-delivered edited document is skipped, so streams that carry updates need a
version-aware id. The filter options (`includeId`, `excludeId`, `minDocumentSize`,
`documentFilter`) answer rejected deliveries with a filtered outcome that never keeps
a dedup claim.

With `modality` set to `media` the payload (audio, an image, video or a PDF) is embedded
whole, as one vector; the source must deliver raw bytes. A file source re-polls any
document that fails the exchange on every run, so restrict the ids with `includeId` or
the source's `include`.

For a Microsoft 365 mailbox that needs an OAuth login, use `ms-exchange-online-imap-oauth-source`, and for Gmail through its API, use `google-mail-source`.

Output: the body is the text of the email. For an email with several parts, such as text and HTML or attachments, it is the text of the first part; attachments are not in the body. The `ce-subject`, `ce-from`, `ce-to` and `ce-cc` headers hold the subject and the addresses, and the headers of the email, such as `Subject`, `From`, `Date` and `Message-ID`, are copied too.

Good to know: emails stay in the mailbox, marked as read, and emails that are already read are skipped. It reads only the `INBOX` folder. It always connects with TLS (IMAPS) and checks the certificate of the server. It checks for new email once a minute by default (`delay`).

kamelets.name: mail-sink
kamelets.title: Mail Sink
kamelets.summary: Sends each message as an email through an SMTP server, with the body as the text of the email.
kamelets.description:
Sends each message as an email through an SMTP server, with the body as the text of the email.

Use it to send notifications, alerts or reports by email, for example tell a team when an order fails or send a daily summary.

Input: the body is the text of the email. With a `Content-Type` header of `text/html`, the email is sent as HTML. The `ce-subject`, `ce-from`, `ce-to` and `ce-cc` headers set the subject, the sender, the recipients and the copy recipients of one email, in place of the options; several addresses are separated by commas. Other mail headers on the message, such as `To` or `Bcc`, are removed and not used.

Output: the message is unchanged. The `CamelMailMessageId` header holds the ID of the email that was sent.

Good to know: set `from`, `to` and `subject`, even though they are not marked as required: the Kamelet does not start without them. The default protocol, `smtps`, connects with TLS and checks the certificate of the server. With `smtp`, the connection, the password and the emails are not encrypted.

kamelets.name: mask-field-action
kamelets.title: Mask Fields Action
kamelets.summary: Replaces the values of the fields you name in each message that is a JSON object with a fixed value, such as `XXXX`.
kamelets.description:
Replaces the values of the fields you name in each message that is a JSON object with a fixed value, such as `XXXX`.

Use it to hide card numbers, passwords or personal data before the messages are logged or sent to another system. To remove a field entirely, use `drop-field-action`, or `replace-field-action` for several fields.

Input: a JSON object, as JSON text or as parsed JSON (a Map or a Jackson `JsonNode`). Only the fields at the top level of the object are masked; nested objects are left as they are. A JSON array, or a body that is not JSON, fails.

Output: the object with the masked values; the order of its fields can change. When the `Content-Type` header is `application/json`, the body is JSON text again; otherwise it is parsed JSON (a Jackson `JsonNode`), which `json-serialize-action` turns into JSON text.

Good to know: the replacement must suit the value it replaces. A text value takes any replacement, but a number takes only a number, such as `0`, and a true or false value, an object or a list cannot be masked: such a message fails. A named field that the object does not have is ignored.

kamelets.name: message-timestamp-router-action
kamelets.title: Message Timestamp Router Action
kamelets.summary: Changes the topic that `kafka-sink` writes a record to, to a name made of the original topic name and a date read from a field of the JSON body.
kamelets.description:
Changes the topic that `kafka-sink` writes a record to, to a name made of the original topic name and a date read from a field of the JSON body.

Use it to spread the records over one topic per day or per month by a date in the data, such as the date of an order, in a flow from `kafka-source` to `kafka-sink`. To use the time the record was written to Kafka instead use `timestamp-router-action`.

Input: a JSON object as JSON text, with the `Content-Type` header set to `application/json`. The name of the topic is read from the `CamelKafkaTopic` header, which `kafka-source` sets.

Output: the same JSON object, as JSON text in a stream, with `Content-Type` set to `application/json`. When one of the `timestampKeys` fields is found, the `CamelKafkaOverrideTopic` header is set to the new name, and `kafka-sink` writes the record to that topic instead of its own `topic`.

Good to know: a field value that cannot be read as a date with `timestampKeyFormat` makes the message fail. The default `topicFormat` of `topic-$[timestamp]` gives names such as `topic-20240703`, without the original name: set it to `$[topic]-$[timestamp]` to keep it. The date is in UTC.

kamelets.name: minio-sink
kamelets.title: Minio Sink
kamelets.summary: Uploads each message as a file (object) to a bucket in MinIO, the S3-compatible object storage.
kamelets.description:
Uploads each message as a file (object) to a bucket in MinIO, the S3-compatible object storage.

Use it to store data in MinIO, such as reports, exports, images or received messages to keep as an archive. For Amazon S3 use `aws-s3-sink`, and for the S3 gateway of Ceph use `ceph-sink`.

Input: the body is the content of the file, as text, bytes or a stream. When `keyName` is set, every message is stored under that name. Otherwise the name of the file comes from the optional `file` header, or the `ce-file` header, and is a generated unique name when neither is set.

Output: the body is unchanged. The `CamelMinioObjectName` header holds the name the file was stored under, unless `keyName` is set.

Good to know: a file with the same name is overwritten, so with `keyName` set each message replaces the previous one. When `keyName` is set, the `file` and `ce-file` headers are ignored.

kamelets.name: minio-source
kamelets.title: Minio Source
kamelets.summary: Reads the files (objects) in a MinIO bucket, one message per file, and by default deletes each file once it has been read.
kamelets.description:
Reads the files (objects) in a MinIO bucket, one message per file, and by default deletes each file once it has been read.

Use it to process files that another system drops into a MinIO bucket, such as uploaded documents, exported reports or log files. For Amazon S3 use `aws-s3-source`, and for the S3 gateway of Ceph use `ceph-source`.

Output: the body is the content of the file, as bytes. The headers give the bucket name, the name of the file (`CamelMinioObjectName`), and its content type, size, ETag and last modified date.

Good to know: files are deleted from the bucket after they are read, unless `deleteAfterRead` is set to false; then the same files are read again on every poll, about twice a second. Only the files at the top of the bucket are read: a file in a folder, such as `reports/january.csv`, is not.

kamelets.description:
Reads the unread emails in the inbox of a Microsoft 365 (Exchange Online) mailbox over IMAP, logging in with OAuth 2.0, and marks each email as read.

Use it to process the email that arrives in a Microsoft 365 mailbox where login with a password is turned off, for example orders, invoices or support requests sent to a shared address. For other mail servers, use `mail-imap-source`.

Output: the body is the text of the email. Good to know: it logs in as an application, not as a person: register an application in Microsoft Entra ID (formerly Azure Active Directory) with a client secret, and allow it to read the mailbox over IMAP. It gets a token when it starts, so with wrong credentials, such as an unknown tenant ID, the integration does not start. Emails stay in the mailbox, marked as read, and emails that are already read are skipped. It reads only the `INBOX` folder, over TLS, and checks for new email once a minute by default (`delay`).

kamelets.name: mustache-template-action
kamelets.title: Mustache Template Action
kamelets.summary: Builds a new message body from a Mustache template, filling in values from the incoming message.
kamelets.description:
Builds a new message body from a Mustache template, filling in values from the incoming message.

Use it to turn data into text for people or for another system, such as the text of an email or a chat message, or a small JSON or XML document, without writing code. To reshape JSON into other JSON, `jsonata-action` or `jslt-action` is often simpler.

Input: any body. The template sees the body as `{\{body}}` and a header as `{{headers.name}}`.

Output: the body is the text the template produced. The headers are kept.

Good to know: the template is loaded from a file, the classpath or a URL given by the `template` option; it cannot come from the message.

kamelets.name: mvel-template-action
kamelets.title: Mvel Template Action
kamelets.summary: Builds a new message body from an MVEL template, filling in values from the incoming message.
kamelets.description:
Builds a new message body from an MVEL template, filling in values from the incoming message.

Use it to turn data into text for people or for another system, such as the text of an email or a small XML or JSON document, when you already have MVEL templates. For simple templates, `mustache-template-action` is an alternative; to reshape JSON into other JSON, `jslt-action` is often simpler.

Input: any body. The template sees the body as `@\{body}` and a header as `@{headers.name}`, for example `Dear @{headers.customer}, your order @\{body} has shipped.`

Output: the body is the text the template produced. The headers are kept.

Good to know: a header the template uses that is not set fails the message, and so does a template file that cannot be found. The template is loaded from a file, the classpath or a URL given by the `template` option; it cannot come from the message.

kamelets.description:
Keeps only the JSON messages that match a condition, written as a JSONPath expression, and drops all others.

Use it to pass on only the messages you care about, for example only the orders above a certain amount, or only the events of one customer. To keep or drop messages by a header, use `header-matches-filter-action` or `has-header-filter-action` instead.

Input: a JSON object, as JSON text or as parsed JSON.

Output: the same message, unchanged, when the condition is true. When it is false, the message is dropped and nothing is sent on.

Good to know: a message that does not have the field the condition looks at is dropped too.

kamelets.name: protobuf-deserialize-action
kamelets.title: Protobuf Deserialize Action
kamelets.summary: Turns each message of Protobuf binary data back into a JSON object, using the Protobuf schema the data was written with.
kamelets.description:
Turns each message of Protobuf binary data back into a JSON object, using the Protobuf schema the data was written with.

Use it to read records that arrive in Protocol Buffers (Protobuf), a compact binary format described by a schema, and work on them as JSON. To turn JSON into Protobuf, use `protobuf-serialize-action`; for Avro, use `avro-deserialize-action`.

Input: Protobuf binary data, as bytes, such as `protobuf-serialize-action` writes.

Output: the body is parsed JSON (a Jackson `JsonNode`) with the fields found in the data. The `Content-Type` header is removed. Put `json-serialize-action` after this action to get JSON text.

Good to know: a body that is not Protobuf data, such as JSON text, fails. When `schema` is not set, the schema found by an earlier `resolve-pojo-schema-action` is used.

kamelets.name: protobuf-serialize-action
kamelets.title: Protobuf Serialize Action
kamelets.summary: Turns each message, a JSON object, into Protobuf binary data that follows the Protobuf schema you give.
kamelets.description:
Turns each message, a JSON object, into Protobuf binary data that follows the Protobuf schema you give.

Use it to send records in Protocol Buffers (Protobuf), a compact binary format described by a schema, to a system that expects it, such as a Kafka topic whose readers decode Protobuf. To turn Protobuf back into JSON, use `protobuf-deserialize-action`; for Avro, use `avro-serialize-action`.

Input: parsed JSON (a Map or a Jackson `JsonNode`) whose fields match the schema. Put `json-deserialize-action` before this action when the body is JSON text.

Output: the body is the Protobuf binary data, as bytes, and the `Content-Type` header is set to `application/protobuf`.

Good to know: JSON text is not turned into Protobuf: it is passed on as it is, yet the `Content-Type` header is set to `application/protobuf`. A message fails when it has a field the schema does not know or a value of the wrong type; a field of the schema that the message lacks is left out, even when it is marked `required`. When `schema` is not set, the schema found by an earlier `resolve-pojo-schema-action` is used.

kamelets.name: regex-router-action
kamelets.title: Regex Router Action
kamelets.summary: Changes the topic that `kafka-sink` writes a record to, by applying a regular expression and a replacement to the name of the topic it was read from.
kamelets.description:
Changes the topic that `kafka-sink` writes a record to, by applying a regular expression and a replacement to the name of the topic it was read from.

Use it to copy records, in a flow from `kafka-source` to `kafka-sink`, to topics with related names, for example from `orders-eu` to `archive-eu`. To add the date to the name use `timestamp-router-action`.

Input: a message from `kafka-source`, with the name of the topic in the `CamelKafkaTopic` header. The same expression is also applied to the `ce-type` header, when there is one.

Output: the same body. When `regex` matches the whole topic name, the `CamelKafkaOverrideTopic` header is set to the name with the match replaced by `replacement`, and `kafka-sink` writes the record to that topic instead of its own `topic`. When `regex` matches the whole `ce-type` header, that header is replaced in the same way.

Good to know: the expression must match the whole name, not a part of it. When it does not match, nothing changes.

kamelets.name: replace-field-action
kamelets.title: Replace Field Action
kamelets.summary: Renames fields of each message that is a JSON object, and can also keep only some fields or remove others.
kamelets.description:
Renames fields of each message that is a JSON object, and can also keep only some fields or remove others.

Use it to match the field names another system expects, such as `name` to `fullName`, and to leave out the fields it should not get. To remove a single field, `drop-field-action` is simpler; to hide a value but keep the field, use `mask-field-action`.

Input: a JSON object, as JSON text or as parsed JSON (a Map or a Jackson `JsonNode`). Only the fields at the top level of the object are renamed, kept or removed; nested objects are left as they are. A JSON array, or a body that is not JSON, fails.

Output: the object with the renamed fields, without the removed ones; the order of its fields can change. When the `Content-Type` header is `application/json`, the body is JSON text again; otherwise it is parsed JSON (a Jackson `JsonNode`), which `json-serialize-action` turns into JSON text.

Good to know: `renames` is required, even when you only want to keep or remove fields. A rename of a field the object does not have is ignored. When `enabled` and `disabled` together would remove every field, the object is passed on unchanged.

kamelets.name: resolve-pojo-schema-action
kamelets.title: Resolve Schema Action
kamelets.summary: Attaches an Avro, Protobuf or JSON schema to each message, for the later steps that need one, and leaves the body unchanged.
kamelets.description:
Attaches an Avro, Protobuf or JSON schema to each message, for the later steps that need one, and leaves the body unchanged.

Use it to give the schema once, before `data-type-action` with a format such as `avro-binary` or `protobuf-binary`, which takes its schema only from here. `avro-serialize-action`, `avro-deserialize-action`, `protobuf-serialize-action` and `protobuf-deserialize-action` use it too when their own `schema` is not set.

Input: any body. The schema comes from `schema`, or else from the Java class named by `contentClass`.

Output: the body and the headers are unchanged. The schema is kept with the message in the properties `X-Content-Schema` and `X-Content-Schema-Type` (`avsc`, `proto` or `json`), which are not headers and are not sent to other systems.

Good to know: with the default `mimeType`, `application/json`, and no `schema` or `contentClass`, it does nothing. A `mimeType` it does not know makes every message fail with "Unsupported type".

kamelets.name: rest-openapi-sink
kamelets.title: REST OpenAPI Sink
kamelets.summary: Calls one operation of a REST API for each message, building the request (method, path, parameters and content type) from the OpenAPI specification of the API.
kamelets.description:
Calls one operation of a REST API for each message, building the request (method, path, parameters and content type) from the OpenAPI specification of the API.

Use it to call an API that publishes an OpenAPI (Swagger) document without writing its URLs by hand, for example to create a customer or look up an order in a service of your company. For a call to a fixed URL, use `http-sink`, or `http-secured-sink` when the service needs a login.

Input: the body is the request body, such as JSON text, and is sent with the content type the specification gives for the operation. The path and query parameters of the operation come from headers of the same name: for `/pets/\{petId}`, set the `petId` header. The other headers of the message, except the Camel ones, are sent as HTTP headers.

Output: when it is used inside a route, the body afterwards is the response of the API, as bytes, with the headers of the response and its status code in `CamelHttpResponseCode`.

Good to know: a missing path parameter is not an error; the request is sent with `\{petId}` in the path. The address of the API is taken from the `servers` of the specification, unless `host` or `basePath` is set. The Kamelet has no login options. The Kamelet does not start when the specification has no operation with the ID in `operation`.

kamelets.name: salesforce-composite-upsert-sink
kamelets.title: Salesforce composite upsert Sink
kamelets.summary: Creates or updates many Salesforce records of one kind in a single call, matching each record to an existing one by an external ID field.
kamelets.description:
Creates or updates many Salesforce records of one kind in a single call, matching each record to an existing one by an external ID field.

Use it to copy a batch of customers, products or orders from another system into Salesforce without creating duplicates: a record whose external ID is already in Salesforce is updated, the others are created. To create or change one record at a time, use `salesforce-create-sink` or `salesforce-update-sink`.

Input: the body is JSON text with a `records` list. Each record gives its kind in `attributes`, such as `{"attributes": {"type": "Contact"}, "External_Id__c": "C-1", "LastName": "Lovelace"}`, and holds the external ID field named by `sObjectIdName` with its value, and the fields to set. Salesforce accepts up to 200 records in one call.

Output: when it is used inside a route, the body afterwards is a List with one result per record, in the same order, each with `id`, `success`, `created` (true for a new record) and `errors`.

Good to know: a record that Salesforce refuses does not fail the message, and the other records are still saved: check `success` in the results.

kamelets.name: salesforce-create-sink
kamelets.title: Salesforce Create Sink
kamelets.summary: Creates a new record, such as a contact, an account or a lead, in Salesforce for each message.
kamelets.description:
Creates a new record, such as a contact, an account or a lead, in Salesforce for each message.

Use it to add to Salesforce what happens in other systems, for example a contact for each web form sent or a lead from a marketing tool. To change existing records use `salesforce-update-sink`, and to create or update many records at once, matched by an external ID, `salesforce-composite-upsert-sink`.

Input: the body is the fields of the new record as JSON text, with the API names of the fields, such as `{"LastName": "Lovelace", "Email": "ada@example.com"}`. It is sent to Salesforce as it is. The kind of record comes from `sObjectName`.

Output: when it is used inside a route, the body afterwards is the answer of Salesforce as JSON text, with the `id` of the new record, `success` and `errors`.

Good to know: a record that Salesforce refuses, for example because a required field is missing or a validation rule fails, fails the message. `sObjectName` must be set, or the Kamelet does not start.

kamelets.name: salesforce-delete-sink
kamelets.title: Salesforce Delete Sink
kamelets.summary: Deletes the Salesforce record that each message names by its ID, such as a contact or an account.
kamelets.description:
Deletes the Salesforce record that each message names by its ID, such as a contact or an account.

Use it to remove records from Salesforce when they are removed in another system, for example to delete a contact when a customer closes their account.

Input: the body is JSON text with two fields: `sObjectName`, the API name of the kind of record (such as `Contact`), and `sObjectId`, the ID of the record. For example `{"sObjectName": "Contact", "sObjectId": "003XXXXXXXXXXXXXXX"}`. Other fields are ignored.

Output: when it is used inside a route, the body afterwards is empty.

Good to know: Salesforce moves the deleted record to its Recycle Bin. A message without `sObjectName` or `sObjectId`, or for a record that does not exist, fails. The message decides which record is deleted, so place this sink only after a source you trust.

kamelets.name: salesforce-pubsub-source
kamelets.title: Salesforce Pub/Sub Source
kamelets.summary: Receives the events of a Salesforce channel, such as a Platform Event or the Change Data Capture events of a kind of record, through the Pub/Sub API, one message per event.
kamelets.description:
Receives the events of a Salesforce channel, such as a Platform Event or the Change Data Capture events of a kind of record, through the Pub/Sub API, one message per event.

Use it to react to what happens in Salesforce, for example to an `Order_Shipped__e` Platform Event that a Flow publishes, or to every change of an account through `/data/AccountChangeEvent`. To be told about records that match a SOQL query, through a PushTopic, use `salesforce-source`.

Output: by default (`deserializeType` `JSON`) the body is the event as JSON text, with the fields of the event. The `CamelSalesforcePubSubReplayId` header holds the replay ID of the event, and `CamelSalesforcePubSubEventId` its ID.

Good to know: by default only the events published after the start are received. The Kamelet does not remember where it stopped: to go on after a restart, set `replayPreset` to `CUSTOM` and `replayId` to the replay ID of the last event processed.

kamelets.name: salesforce-source
kamelets.title: Salesforce Source
kamelets.summary: Receives an event each time a Salesforce record that matches a SOQL query is created, updated, deleted or undeleted, through a PushTopic of the Streaming API.
kamelets.description:
Receives an event each time a Salesforce record that matches a SOQL query is created, updated, deleted or undeleted, through a PushTopic of the Streaming API.

Use it to react to changes in Salesforce, for example to copy each new contact to a mailing tool or to alert a team when an opportunity is won. For Platform Events and Change Data Capture through the newer Pub/Sub API, use `salesforce-pubsub-source`.

Output: the body is the record as JSON text, with the fields that the query selects. The `CamelSalesforceEventType` header says what happened: `created`, `updated`, `deleted` or `undeleted`. The `CamelSalesforceReplayId` header identifies the event.

Good to know: when it starts, it creates the PushTopic `topicName` in Salesforce with `query` and the notify options, or updates it when it exists, so the user needs the permission to create PushTopics. By default only new records send an event; turn on `notifyForOperationUpdate` and the others for more. Only the events after the start are received, unless `replayId` is set.

kamelets.name: salesforce-update-sink
kamelets.title: Salesforce Update Sink
kamelets.summary: Changes fields of an existing Salesforce record, such as the phone number of a contact, for each message; the message names the record and the new values.
kamelets.description:
Changes fields of an existing Salesforce record, such as the phone number of a contact, for each message; the message names the record and the new values.

Use it to keep Salesforce records in step with another system, for example to update the address of an account when it changes in the ERP. To create records use `salesforce-create-sink`, and to create or update many records matched by an external ID, `salesforce-composite-upsert-sink`.

Input: the body is JSON text with three fields: `sObjectName`, the API name of the kind of record (such as `Contact`); `sObjectId`, the ID of the record; and `payload`, an object with the fields to change and their new values. For example `{"sObjectName": "Contact", "sObjectId": "003XXXXXXXXXXXXXXX", "payload": {"Phone": "+45 1234 5678"}}`. The fields that are not in `payload` keep their values.

Output: when it is used inside a route, the body afterwards is the `payload` as JSON text.

Good to know: a message without `sObjectName` or `sObjectId`, for a record that does not exist, or with a change that Salesforce refuses, fails. The message decides which record is changed, so place this sink only after a source you trust.

kamelets.name: sap-netweaver-sink
kamelets.title: SAP NetWeaver Sink
kamelets.summary: Send requests to an SAP NetWeaver Gateway over HTTP.
kamelets.description: Send requests to an SAP NetWeaver Gateway over HTTP.

kamelets.name: scp-sink
kamelets.title: SCP Sink
kamelets.summary: Copies each message as a file to the home directory of a user on a remote server, with SCP (secure copy) over an SSH connection.
kamelets.description:
Copies each message as a file to the home directory of a user on a remote server, with SCP (secure copy) over an SSH connection.

Use it to copy files to a server you reach with SSH that does not offer SFTP, for example to drop a configuration or a report on a host. To choose the directory on the server, or to append to or keep existing files, use `sftp-sink` instead.

Input: the body is the content of the file, as text, bytes or a stream. The name of the file comes from the `CamelFileName` header, which may hold subdirectories, such as `reports/data.csv`; without it, a unique name is generated.

Output: the message is unchanged.

Good to know: files are written in the home directory of `username`, with the rights of that user, and a file with the same name is replaced. A file name that points outside the home directory fails the message. The key of the server is checked against `~/.ssh/known_hosts` of the user that runs the integration, unless `strictHostKeyChecking` is `no`. Setting `knownHostsUri` or `privateKeyPassphrase` stops the Kamelet from starting. Do not place it after messages from an untrusted source.

kamelets.name: set-body-action
kamelets.title: Set Body Action
kamelets.summary: Replaces the body of each message with a text you write, which can include values from the message, such as a header.
kamelets.description:
Replaces the body of each message with a text you write, which can include values from the message, such as a header.

Use it to send a fixed text or a small JSON document, such as a status message, or to build a short text from headers and the old body. For longer texts, a template Kamelet such as `mustache-template-action` is easier to maintain.

Input: any message. In the text, `$\{body}` is the old body and `${header.name}` the value of a header.

Output: the body is the text, with the values filled in. The headers are kept as they were, `Content-Type` too, so set it to match the new body when needed, for example with `insert-header-action`.

Good to know: up to Camel 4.23, two closing braces in a row are read as the end of a placeholder and make the Kamelet fail to start, so write nested JSON with a space between them, as `} }`.

kamelets.name: set-kafka-key-action
kamelets.title: Set Kafka Key Action
kamelets.summary: Sets the key of the Kafka record to the value of a header of the message.
kamelets.description:
Sets the key of the Kafka record to the value of a header of the message.

Use it before `kafka-sink` when the records need a key, for example so that all the records of one customer go to the same partition and stay in order.

Input: any message with the header named by `headerName`.

Output: the same body. The `CamelKafkaKey` header, which `kafka-sink` uses as the record key, is set to the value of that header.

Good to know: to build the key from fields of the body instead, use `value-to-key-action`.

kamelets.name: sftp-sink
kamelets.title: SFTP Sink
kamelets.summary: Uploads each message as a file to a directory on an SFTP server, which transfers files over an encrypted SSH connection.
kamelets.description:
Uploads each message as a file to a directory on an SFTP server, which transfers files over an encrypted SSH connection.

Use it to deliver exports, reports or data files to a server you reach with SSH, such as the SFTP drop box of a partner. For an FTP server use `ftp-sink` or `ftps-sink`.

Input: the body is the content of the file, as text, bytes or a stream. The name of the file comes from the `file` header, or from `ce-file` when `file` is not set; any directory in it is dropped, so `reports/data.csv` is written as `data.csv`. Without these headers, `CamelFileName` is used as it is, subdirectories included, and without any of them a unique name is generated.

Output: the message is unchanged. The `CamelFileNameProduced` header is set to the path of the file on the server.

Good to know: a file with the same name is replaced, unless `fileExist` says otherwise. Log in with `username` and either `password` or a private key. The key of the server must be in a known_hosts file, `knownHostsUri` or else `~/.ssh/known_hosts` of the user that runs the integration, or the connection fails. A file name that points outside `directoryName` fails the message.

kamelets.name: sftp-source
kamelets.title: SFTP Source
kamelets.summary: Reads the files in a directory on an SFTP server, over an encrypted SSH connection, one message per file, and by default leaves them on the server.
kamelets.description:
Reads the files in a directory on an SFTP server, over an encrypted SSH connection, one message per file, and by default leaves them on the server.

Use it to collect the files that a partner or another system drops on a server you reach with SSH, such as orders, invoices or exports. For an FTP server use `ftp-source` or `ftps-source`.

Output: the body is the content of the file, as bytes. The `file` and `ce-file` headers hold the name of the file, with its path below `directoryName` when `recursive` is true, such as `2026/orders.csv`. `CamelFileName` holds the same name, and `CamelFileLength` the size of the file in bytes.

Good to know: files are not deleted or moved after they are read, unless `delete` is true. A file is read only once while the integration runs (`idempotent`), but the files left on the server are all read again after a restart; set `delete` to true to read each file only once. Log in with `username` and either `password` or a private key. The key of the server must be in a known_hosts file, `knownHostsUri` or else `~/.ssh/known_hosts` of the user that runs the integration, or the connection fails.

kamelets.name: simple-filter-action
kamelets.title: Simple Filter Action
kamelets.summary: Drops the messages for which a condition, written in the Camel Simple language, is true, and passes on all others.
kamelets.description:
Drops the messages for which a condition, written in the Camel Simple language, is true, and passes on all others.

Use it to leave out the messages you do not want, for example the test events, with the condition `${header.type} == 'test'`. To keep only the messages that match a condition instead, use `predicate-filter-action` (a condition on a JSON body), `has-header-filter-action` or `header-matches-filter-action`.

Input: any message.

Output: the same message, unchanged, when the condition is false. When it is true, the message is dropped and nothing is sent on.

Good to know: this is the opposite of the other filter actions of the catalog, which keep the messages that match. A condition on a header the message does not have is false, so such a message is passed on.

kamelets.name: slack-sink
kamelets.title: Slack Sink
kamelets.summary: Posts each message as a text message to a Slack channel, through an incoming webhook of a Slack app.
kamelets.description:
Posts each message as a text message to a Slack channel, through an incoming webhook of a Slack app.

Use it to tell a team in Slack when something happens, such as a monitoring alert, a failed build, a new order or a daily report. To read the messages of a channel instead, use `slack-source`.

Input: the body is the text of the Slack message, as text; another kind of body is turned into text first. JSON text is posted as it is, as the text of the message, not as a Slack message structure. The text can use Slack's own formatting, such as `*bold*`. Headers are not read.

Output: the message is unchanged.

Good to know: the webhook decides where the message goes. The webhook of a Slack app posts only to the channel chosen when the webhook was created, whatever `channel` says. When Slack does not answer with a success status, the message fails.

kamelets.name: slack-source
kamelets.title: Slack Source
kamelets.summary: Reads the new messages posted in a public Slack channel, by asking Slack at a regular interval, one message per Slack message.
kamelets.description:
Reads the new messages posted in a public Slack channel, by asking Slack at a regular interval, one message per Slack message.

Use it to react to what people write in a channel, for example to turn a message in `#support` into a ticket, to archive a channel, or to start a job when someone posts a command. To post to Slack instead, use `slack-sink`.

Output: the body is the Slack message as JSON text, with fields such as `text` (what was written), `user` (the ID of the author) and `ts` (the time stamp that identifies the message). The `Content-Type` header is `application/json`.

Good to know: when it starts, it also sends the most recent message already in the channel, then only the messages posted after it. It does not remember where it stopped: after a restart it starts again from the most recent message. It reads public channels only, by their name, and needs a token of a Slack app, see `token`.

kamelets.summary: Send SMS messages through a SMSC (Short Message Service Center) using the SMPP protocol.

kamelets.name: solr-source
kamelets.title: Solr Source
kamelets.summary: Runs the same query on a collection or core of Apache Solr at a regular interval, and sends the result of each query as one message.
kamelets.description:
Runs the same query on a collection or core of Apache Solr at a regular interval, and sends the result of each query as one message.

Use it to watch a Solr collection on a schedule, for example to send the documents that match a query to another system. To add documents to Solr, use `solr-sink`.

Output: the body is JSON text, the answer of Solr: `responseHeader`, and under `response` the list of the documents found, each with its fields. The `Content-Type` header is `application/json`.

Good to know: every query returns all the matching documents again, not only the new ones; filter on a date in the query to get only new documents. Each query returns only the first documents found, 10 with the usual Solr settings. It connects with plain HTTP.

kamelets.title: Microsoft SQL Server Sink
kamelets.summary: Send data to a Microsoft SQL Server Database. This Kamelet expects a JSON-formatted body. Use key:value pairs to map the JSON fields and parameters.
kamelets.description: Send data to a Microsoft SQL Server Database. This Kamelet expects a JSON-formatted body. Use key:value pairs to map the JSON fields and parameters.
