kamelets.name: ssh-sink
kamelets.title: SSH Sink
kamelets.summary: Runs the text of each message as a command on a remote server over SSH, and returns what the command prints.
kamelets.description:
Runs the text of each message as a command on a remote server over SSH, and returns what the command prints.

Use it to run a script or a maintenance command on a server when something happens, for example restart a service after a deployment or clear a cache when data changes. To run a fixed command on a schedule and read its output, use `ssh-source`; to run a command on the machine of the integration, use `exec-sink`.

Input: the body is the command to run, as text, such as `systemctl restart myapp`. It runs in the shell of `username`, so it can hold several commands separated by `;`.

Output: the body afterwards is what the command printed on its standard output, as a stream. The `CamelSshExitValue` header holds the exit code of the command, and `CamelSshStderr` what it printed on its standard error, as a stream.

Good to know: it runs whatever command it receives, with the rights of `username`. Never send it messages from an untrusted source, and log in with an account that may do only what is needed. A command that ends with an exit code other than 0 does not fail the message: check `CamelSshExitValue`. The key of the server is checked only when `knownHostsResource` is set; without it, any server is accepted.

kamelets.name: ssh-source
kamelets.title: SSH Source
kamelets.summary: Runs a command on a remote server over SSH again and again, at a regular interval, and sends what the command prints as a message each time.
kamelets.description:
Runs a command on a remote server over SSH again and again, at a regular interval, and sends what the command prints as a message each time.

Use it to watch a server without installing anything on it, for example check the free disk space, the state of a service or the last lines of a log file every minute. To run a command for each incoming message instead, use `ssh-sink`.

Output: the body is what the command printed on its standard output, as text. The `CamelSshExitValue` header holds the exit code of the command, and `CamelSshStderr` what it printed on its standard error, as a stream.

Good to know: it runs `pollCommand` with the rights of `username`, so log in with an account that may do only what is needed. It runs it every half second by default; set `delay` to how often you need it. A command that fails still sends a message, with its exit code in `CamelSshExitValue`. The key of the server is checked only when `knownHostsResource` is set; without it, any server is accepted.

kamelets.name: string-template-action
kamelets.title: String Template Action
kamelets.summary: Builds a new message body from a StringTemplate template, filling in values from the incoming message.
kamelets.description:
Builds a new message body from a StringTemplate template, filling in values from the incoming message.

Use it to turn data into text for people or for another system, such as the text of an email or a small XML or JSON document, when you already have StringTemplate templates. For simple templates, `mustache-template-action` is an alternative; to reshape JSON into other JSON, `jslt-action` is often simpler.

Input: any body. The template sees the body as `<body>` and a header as `<headers.name>`, for example `Dear <headers.customer>, your order <body> has shipped.`

Output: the body is the text the template produced. The headers are kept, and a `CamelStringTemplateResourceUri` header is added with the location of the template.

Good to know: a header the template uses that is not set gives nothing in the text. A template file that cannot be found fails the message. The template is loaded from a file, the classpath or a URL given by the `template` option; it cannot come from the message.

kamelets.name: telegram-sink
kamelets.title: Telegram Sink
kamelets.summary: Sends each message as a text message, or as a photo, from your Telegram bot to a Telegram chat, group or channel.
kamelets.description:
Sends each message as a text message, or as a photo, from your Telegram bot to a Telegram chat, group or channel.

Use it to notify a person or a group on Telegram, for example with an alert, an order update or a daily report, or to answer the messages your bot receives with `telegram-source`.

Input: the body is the text of the message, as text; another kind of body is turned into text first, and the text is sent as it is, without Markdown or HTML formatting. When the `Content-Type` header is `image/png` or `image/jpeg`, the body is sent as a photo instead, as bytes, and the `text` or `ce-text` header is its caption. The `chat-id` or `ce-chatid` header chooses the chat, instead of the `chatId` option; `telegram-source` sets both, so a reply goes back to the chat a message came from.

Output: when it is used inside a route, the body afterwards is the answer of Telegram as JSON text, with the message that was sent.

Good to know: a message fails when no chat is given, neither in a header nor in `chatId`, and when Telegram refuses it, for example because the bot is not a member of the group or the person never started a chat with the bot.

kamelets.name: telegram-source
kamelets.title: Telegram Source
kamelets.summary: Receives the messages that people send to your Telegram bot, in private chats and in the groups the bot is in, one message per Telegram message.
kamelets.description:
Receives the messages that people send to your Telegram bot, in private chats and in the groups the bot is in, one message per Telegram message.

Use it to build a chat bot, for example to answer questions, take orders or run commands sent on Telegram; send the answers with `telegram-sink`.

Output: the body is the Telegram message as JSON text, with fields such as `text` (what was written), `chat` (with the `id` of the chat), `from` (the sender) and `message_id`. A photo or a document comes without `text`. The `chat-id` and `ce-chatid` headers hold the ID of the chat, so that `telegram-sink` can answer in the same chat.

Good to know: it asks Telegram for new messages all the time, and each message is received once. Telegram keeps the messages that arrive while the Kamelet is stopped for up to 24 hours. It does not work while a webhook is set for the bot, and only one application at a time can read the messages of a bot. In a group, Telegram gives a bot only the commands and the replies to the bot, unless its privacy mode is turned off with @BotFather.

kamelets.name: throttle-action
kamelets.title: Throttle Action
kamelets.summary: Lets through at most a set number of messages per period of time, such as 10 per second, and holds back the rest for a later period.
kamelets.description:
Lets through at most a set number of messages per period of time, such as 10 per second, and holds back the rest for a later period.

Use it to protect a sink or a service that cannot take more than a certain rate, for example an API that allows 100 calls per minute. To hold every message for a fixed time instead, use `delay-action`.

Input: any message.

Output: the same message, unchanged. The messages over the limit are not dropped: they wait, and are passed on in a later period.

kamelets.name: tika-extract-text-action
kamelets.title: Tika Extract Text Action
kamelets.summary: Extract plain text from PDF, office and similar documents in-process with Apache Tika.
kamelets.description:
Extract plain text from PDF, office and similar documents in-process with Apache Tika.

Before the parse, the value of the `documentIdHeader` header is captured into the
`CamelLangChain4jIngestDocumentId` exchange property - Tika copies document metadata
over the headers, so a crafted document could otherwise forge its own identity in steps
that read it later (the langchain4j-ingest sink does). The extracted text is decoded at
a pinned UTF-8 (a document-injected charset header is swept before the conversion), and
after the parse all non-Camel headers are removed: past this action, parsed document
metadata is indistinguishable from caller headers, so it must not travel further. Each
format needs its Tika parser module on the classpath; camel-tika ships the HTML and
text modules, PDF needs org.apache.tika:tika-parser-pdf-module. With `maxDocumentSize`
set, a payload larger than that many bytes fails the exchange before the parse.

kamelets.name: timer-source
kamelets.title: Timer Source
kamelets.summary: Sends the same fixed message again and again at a regular interval, such as once every second.
kamelets.description:
Sends the same fixed message again and again at a regular interval, such as once every second.

Use it to try out a sink or an action without a real system behind it, to trigger a flow on a schedule (for example, call an HTTP service every minute), or to send a heartbeat. For a calendar schedule such as "every weekday at 9:00" use `cron-source` instead, and for a message that counts up use `counter-source`.

Output: the body is the `message` option as text, the same on every message. The `Content-Type` header is set to the `contentType` option.

Good to know: it keeps sending until the integration is stopped, unless `repeatCount` is set.

kamelets.name: timestamp-router-action
kamelets.title: Timestamp Router Action
kamelets.summary: Changes the topic that `kafka-sink` writes a record to, to a name made of the original topic name and the date of the record, such as `orders-20240703`.
kamelets.description:
Changes the topic that `kafka-sink` writes a record to, to a name made of the original topic name and the date of the record, such as `orders-20240703`.

Use it to spread the records over one topic per day or per month, in a flow from `kafka-source` to `kafka-sink`, for example to keep or delete them by period. To take the date from a field of a JSON body instead use `message-timestamp-router-action`.

Input: a message from `kafka-source`, with the name of the topic in the `CamelKafkaTopic` header and the time of the record, in milliseconds since 1970, in the `CamelKafkaTimestamp` header. `topicHeaderName` and `timestampHeaderName` choose other headers.

Output: the same body. The `CamelKafkaOverrideTopic` header is set to the new name, and `kafka-sink` writes the record to that topic instead of its own `topic`.

Good to know: the default `topicFormat` of `topic-$[timestamp]` gives names such as `topic-20240703`, without the original name: set it to `$[topic]-$[timestamp]` to keep it. The date is in UTC. Without a time header, nothing changes.

kamelets.name: topic-name-matches-filter-action
kamelets.title: Kafka Topic Name Matches Filter Action
kamelets.summary: Keeps only the Kafka records whose topic name matches a regular expression, and drops all others.
kamelets.description:
Keeps only the Kafka records whose topic name matches a regular expression, and drops all others.

Use it to handle the records of only some topics, after a `kafka-source` whose `topic` lists several topics or is a pattern, for example only those of `orders-eu`. To keep or drop messages by another header use `header-matches-filter-action`.

Input: a message from `kafka-source`, with the name of the topic in the `CamelKafkaTopic` header.

Output: the same message, unchanged, when `regex` matches the whole topic name. Otherwise the message is dropped and nothing is sent on.

Good to know: the expression must match the whole name: `orders` does not keep the records of `orders-eu`, but `orders.*` does. A message without the `CamelKafkaTopic` header is dropped.

kamelets.name: twitter-directmessage-source
kamelets.title: Twitter Direct Message Source
kamelets.summary: Reads the direct messages of a Twitter (X) account, by asking Twitter at a regular interval, one message per direct message.
kamelets.description:
Reads the direct messages of a Twitter (X) account, by asking Twitter at a regular interval, one message per direct message.

Use it to react to private messages sent to your company account, for example to open a support case or to forward them to a team chat. To read public tweets, use `twitter-search-source` or `twitter-timeline-source`.

Output: the body is the direct message as JSON text, with its `text`, its `id`, the `senderId` and the `recipientId`. The `CamelTwitterEventType` header is `DIRECT_MESSAGE`.

Good to know: it reads the messages of the account that owns `accessToken`, both the ones it received and the ones it sent; compare `senderId` to tell them apart. At the first check, every direct message that Twitter still lists (the last 30 days) is sent, then only new ones, every 30 seconds. It does not remember what it read: after a restart, it sends them all again. It uses version 1.1 of the Twitter API, and the app needs the permission to read direct messages.

kamelets.name: twitter-search-source
kamelets.title: Twitter Search Source
kamelets.summary: Reads the new tweets that match a search, such as a word, a hashtag or a mention, by asking Twitter (X) at a regular interval, one message per tweet.
kamelets.description:
Reads the new tweets that match a search, such as a word, a hashtag or a mention, by asking Twitter (X) at a regular interval, one message per tweet.

Use it to follow what people say about a brand, a product or an event, for example to collect mentions for analysis or to alert a team. To follow the tweets of one account, use `twitter-timeline-source`.

Output: the body is the tweet as JSON text, with its `text`, its `id`, its `lang`, the time it was created and the `user` who wrote it. The `CamelTwitterEventType` header is `STATUS`.

Good to know: it searches every 30 seconds. The first search sends up to 5 matching tweets, and each later search sends at most 5 tweets newer than the last one it saw, so on a busy search some tweets are missed. It does not remember what it read: after a restart, it starts over as on the first search. It uses the standard search of version 1.1 of the Twitter API.

kamelets.name: twitter-timeline-source
kamelets.title: Twitter Timeline Source
kamelets.summary: Reads the new tweets that one Twitter (X) account posts, by asking Twitter at a regular interval, one message per tweet.
kamelets.description:
Reads the new tweets that one Twitter (X) account posts, by asking Twitter at a regular interval, one message per tweet.

Use it to follow an account, such as a news feed, a status page or a partner, and pass on what it posts, for example to a chat or a database. To follow a word or a hashtag across all accounts, use `twitter-search-source`.

Output: the body is the tweet as JSON text, with its `text`, its `id`, the time it was created and the `user` who wrote it. The `CamelTwitterEventType` header is `STATUS`.

Good to know: it checks every 30 seconds. The first check sends the 5 most recent tweets of the account, and each later check sends at most 5 tweets newer than the last one it saw. It does not remember what it read: after a restart, it starts again with the most recent tweets. It uses version 1.1 of the Twitter API.

kamelets.name: value-to-key-action
kamelets.title: Value to Key Action
kamelets.summary: Sets the key of the Kafka record to some fields of the JSON body, so that records with the same values in those fields get the same key.
kamelets.description:
Sets the key of the Kafka record to some fields of the JSON body, so that records with the same values in those fields get the same key.

Use it to take the key of the record from the data, before `kafka-sink`, for example the customer of an order, so that all the records of one customer go to the same partition and stay in order. To take the key from a header instead use `set-kafka-key-action`.

Input: a JSON object as JSON text, with the `Content-Type` header set to `application/json`.

Output: the same JSON object, as JSON text in a stream, with `Content-Type` set to `application/json`. The `CamelKafkaKey` header, which `kafka-sink` uses as the key of the record, is set to a Map of the fields named in `fields` and their values.

Good to know: `kafka-sink` writes the key as text such as `{id=7, customer=acme}`, not as JSON, and not necessarily with the fields in the order of `fields`. A field that is not in the body is left out of the key.

kamelets.name: velocity-template-action
kamelets.title: Velocity Template Action
kamelets.summary: Builds a new message body from an Apache Velocity template, filling in values from the incoming message.
kamelets.description:
Builds a new message body from an Apache Velocity template, filling in values from the incoming message.

Use it to turn data into text for people or for another system, such as an email, a report or a small XML or JSON document, when you already have Velocity templates or need its loops and conditions. For simple templates, `mustache-template-action` is an alternative; to reshape JSON into other JSON, `jslt-action` is often simpler.

Input: any body. The template sees the body as `$\{body}` and a header as `${headers.name}`, for example `Dear ${headers.customer}, your order $\{body} has shipped.`

Output: the body is the text the template produced. The headers are kept.

Good to know: a value the template uses that is missing, such as a header that is not set, stays in the text as written, for example `${headers.customer}`; write `$!{headers.customer}` to get nothing instead. A template file that cannot be found fails the message. The template is loaded from a file, the classpath or a URL given by the `template` option; it cannot come from the message.

kamelets.name: webhook-source
kamelets.title: Webhook Source
kamelets.summary: Receives HTTP requests on a path of its own, such as `/webhook`, and sends each request on as a message, with its body and headers.
kamelets.description:
Receives HTTP requests on a path of its own, such as `/webhook`, and sends each request on as a message, with its body and headers.

Use it to receive the webhook calls of an online service, such as a payment, form or code hosting service, or to let another system push data with a simple HTTP POST. To fetch a URL at a regular interval instead, use `http-source`.

Output: the body is the body of the request, as a stream, and is empty for a request without a body, such as a GET. The HTTP headers of the request become headers of the message, and so does each query parameter. `CamelHttpMethod` gives the method (such as `POST`), `CamelHttpPath` the path and `CamelHttpQuery` the query string. A form (`application/x-www-form-urlencoded`) arrives as a Map of its fields instead.

Good to know: there is no login, so anyone who can reach the address can send messages; protect it with network rules or a gateway in front, and treat the content as untrusted. It accepts every HTTP method, on the exact path only. It listens on the HTTP port of the application, 8080 by default with Camel JBang. The caller gets back the message as it is at the end of the flow: by default the body it sent, with status 200, or status 204 when there is no body.

kamelets.name: wttrin-source
kamelets.title: wttr.in Source
kamelets.summary: Fetches the current weather or the forecast for a place from the public wttr.in service at a regular interval, and sends it as JSON.
kamelets.description:
Fetches the current weather or the forecast for a place from the public wttr.in service at a regular interval, and sends it as JSON.

Use it to feed weather data into a dashboard, a chat message or a decision, such as a frost alert, or as real, changing JSON data for a demo. No account is needed.

Output: the body is JSON text. With `output` set to `current`, the default, it is an object with the current conditions, such as `temp_C`, `humidity` and `weatherDesc`. With `weather`, it is a list with the forecast for each day, starting today. With `full`, it is the whole answer of wttr.in, which has both. The `Content-Type` header is `application/json`, and the other headers of the HTTP answer are kept.

Good to know: it calls `https://wttr.in` over the internet. When `wttrLocation` is not set, wttr.in guesses the place from the IP address of the machine.

kamelets.name: xj-identity-action
kamelets.title: XJ Identity Action
kamelets.summary: Converts each message from XML to JSON, or from JSON to XML, with a fixed mapping and no template to write.
kamelets.description:
Converts each message from XML to JSON, or from JSON to XML, with a fixed mapping and no template to write.

Use it to pass XML to a system that expects JSON, or the other way round, when the default mapping is good enough. To control the result, such as the names of the elements or which fields to keep, use `xj-template-action` with an XSLT stylesheet.

Input: XML or JSON as text, bytes or a stream, as `direction` says. Parsed JSON, such as a Map, fails the message.

Output: the body is JSON text or XML text. From XML, the root element is dropped, its attributes and child elements become fields, repeated elements become an array, and all values are text: `<order id="7"><qty>2</qty></order>` gives `{"id":"7","qty":"2"}`. To XML, each JSON value becomes an `object` element that keeps its name and type in `xj:name` and `xj:type` attributes, such as `<object xj:name="qty" xj:type="int">2</object>`. The headers are kept.

kamelets.name: xj-template-action
kamelets.title: XJ Template Action
kamelets.summary: Converts each message from XML to JSON, or from JSON to XML, with an XSLT stylesheet that decides what the result looks like.
kamelets.description:
Converts each message from XML to JSON, or from JSON to XML, with an XSLT stylesheet that decides what the result looks like.

Use it to map the XML of one system to the JSON of another, or the other way round, when the fixed mapping of `xj-identity-action` does not give the shape you need.

Input: XML or JSON as text, bytes or a stream, as `direction` says. With `JSON2XML` the stylesheet sees the JSON as XML in which each value is an `object` element with its name and type in `xj:name` and `xj:type` attributes, such as `<object xj:name="qty" xj:type="int">2</object>`; select a field with `object[@xj:name='qty']`.

Output: the body is JSON text or XML text. With `XML2JSON` the stylesheet must write that same form, which becomes JSON: `<object xj:type="object"><object xj:name="qty" xj:type="int">2</object></object>` gives `{"qty":2}`. The prefix `xj` stands for the namespace `http://camel.apache.org/component/xj`. The headers are kept.

Good to know: the stylesheet is loaded from a file, the classpath or a URL given by the `template` option; it cannot come from the message.
